title: Book Fourteen begins: coming clean before God
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK FOURTEEN. That those who wish to attend the churches must be clean, washed of the stain that sin leaves, and so present themselves before God.
Cyril: I think I have now said quite enough about the tabernacle, and also about the priests and the service of the Levites, and I believe I have examined these matters closely. It would be fitting…
translator_notes: Section ends mid-word: Πρέ|ποι runs into section 2. The English breaks at 'It would be fitting…' so that each section covers only its own Greek; the sentence continues at the start of section 2. The opening Greek paragraph holds the book title, the chapter summary and Cyril's first words; the English splits title+summary from Cyril's turn, as in the other books. 'ἐκκλησίαι' kept as 'churches' in the summary (Cyril's own application); in the Deuteronomy quotation later the same word is 'assembly'.

title: Coming to God's house cleansed; the unclean sent out of the camp
english: Cyril: …above all for those who choose to live rightly, and to set on their own heads, like a crown, the full beauty of the life lived in Christ, to urge one another on eagerly, as it were, saying: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it’ (Isaiah 2:3). At this some, receiving so glorious and profitable a call, all but leap for joy and say: ‘I was glad when they said to me, “We will go into the house of the Lord”’ (Psalm 122:1). So then, Palladius, for those who hasten to go into the house of God, what would their aim be? Where is their mind looking, and what do they long to accomplish, as they press on toward the holy and divine tabernacle?
Palladius: Well, my friend, the matter is not obscure. For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord in his holy court’ (Psalm 96:9), and: ‘Bring sacrifices, and come into his courts’ (Psalm 96:8).
Cyril: So, then, some enter the house of the Lord and his courts bringing sacrifices on their own behalf, spiritual ones of course, and also intending to draw near in inward worship.
Palladius: That is what I say.

Cyril: Are we then to suppose that those who wish to go in should simply rush in, not washed clean of sin, not freed from vileness, not scraped clean, as it were, of the filth of love for the flesh, but with their mind steeped in it and their heart eaten with rust? Not at all. Rather, they should be adorned with the brightness that is in Christ, and shine with the many-colored beauty of virtue, which is most dear to God.
Palladius: Certainly. For I say that we must come before the eyes of the Lord with every stain first wiped from our thoughts.

Cyril: You are right, since he counts the sick man hateful, and indeed casts him off, and sends him away from the company of the saints. The inspired Paul understood this very well when he wrote: ‘Drive out, then, the wicked person from among you’ (1 Corinthians 5:13). And I would not call this the fruit of a savage temper, but a wise safeguard. ‘For a little leaven,’ he says, ‘leavens the whole lump’ (1 Corinthians 5:6). And again, the sacred law sketched this for us in a riddle. For it is written in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper, and everyone who has a discharge, and everyone who is unclean through a dead body. Male and female alike, send them outside the camp, and they shall not defile their camps, in which I dwell among them. And the sons of Israel did so’ (Numbers 5:1–4). Is it not true to say that the burden of the law is very heavy indeed and truly hard to carry? For you see how it prescribes a penalty even for illnesses that no one chooses, although…
translator_notes: Isaiah 2:3: the wording (ἀναγγελεῖ ἡμῖν) matches Isaiah LXX rather than Micah 4:2 (δείξουσιν). Psalm 122:1 = LXX Psalm 121:1. 'Worship the Lord in his holy court' is identical in LXX Psalm 28:2 (English 29:2) and LXX Psalm 95:9 (English 96:9); cited as Psalm 96:9 because the next line, 'Bring sacrifices and come into his courts', is LXX Psalm 95:8 (English 96:8) from the same psalm; Cyril gives the two verses in reverse order. 1 Corinthians 5:13 itself echoes Deuteronomy 17:7; not cited separately. 1 Corinthians 5:6 also = Galatians 5:9 (same words); Cyril's context is 1 Corinthians 5. Numbers 5:1–4: Cyril reads Λάλησον where LXX has Πρόσταξον; 'unclean upon a soul' (ἀκάθαρτος ἐπὶ ψυχῇ) is the LXX idiom for corpse uncleanness and is rendered 'unclean through a dead body'. νοητὴν προσκύνησιν rendered 'inward worship' (worship grasped by the mind, as against sense). ἐντετηγμένον ἔχοντας τὸν νοῦν (mind melted/softened) rendered 'their mind steeped in it' (the filth just named); the sense could also be 'a mind gone soft'. In 'he counts the sick man hateful' the subject is unstated; most likely the Lord just named, possibly the law. 'The inspired Paul' renders θεσπέσιος. Section ends mid-sentence at καίτοι; the sentence continues in section 3.

title: Why bodily illness barred a person, and what the leper signifies
english: Cyril: …those who have fallen into such misfortunes ought to be pitied. For one might very reasonably wonder why it made the leper an outcast and sent him away, and with him the one held fast by the affliction of a discharge, and again the one unclean through the dead.
Palladius: I could not work it out; perhaps you would explain it yourself.

Cyril: Well, I think that God, as he prefigured for us the divine and spiritual worship, did not take much account of material and bodily matters. For what lies outside the law is punished, and whatever plainly oversteps what is fitting, this I would say falls under judgment and penalty; but a bodily illness could in no way offend against the laws. It will rightly, then, lie far beyond the reach of any charge, and there could be no ground at all for anyone to accuse it. Or is it not plain to everyone that no one is ill by choice, and that everyone, I think, counts good health the thing most to be prayed for?
Palladius: True.

Cyril: So even if the literal history of the passage has something unlovely about it, no harm is done, provided the spiritual meaning is worked out well, in keeping with what the lawgiver intended. Now leprosy is a deadening of the flesh, and an affliction that eats away more than most. That is why the inspired Moses, when Miriam had become leprous, was filled with fear and deep distress, and pleaded, saying: ‘O God, I beg you, heal her’ (Numbers 12:13). For he said: ‘Let her not become like a stillborn child coming out of its mother’s womb, and it will eat away half of her flesh’ (Numbers 12:12). As for the man with a discharge, why should I say what kind of affliction it is? No one is unaware of it. Now as for some being unclean through the dead, this means something like the following. To touch one who has departed and to come near a dead body the law counted, for the people of old, as a kind of defilement (Numbers 19:11), showing that deadness is hateful to God, who has power to give life to all things. It also took the matter in another way, as a rough type of the deadness of mind and soul. And the mind that loves sin, and is used to having no share in the noble deeds that lead to life, is dead and cold. But if someone happened to die, it was altogether necessary that his relatives by blood and family should gather and perform the customary rites over him; yet these too were unclean according to the law, though not for good and for all time, for there was a way for them to be cleansed (Numbers 19:12). There you have a sufficient explanation of the literal history.
Palladius: Quite so.

Cyril: Come, then, let us transpose it into spiritual contemplation and say this: the leper signifies for us the one who is spotted all over with the varied passions of youth. These are the works of the flesh, which the most wise Paul himself listed for us, saying: ‘Sexual immorality, impurity, idolatry, enmities, strife, fits of rage, jealousies’ (Galatians 5:19–20). The second figure, however,…
translator_notes: γραφή here is the legal sense 'indictment', not 'Scripture'. τὸ ἀκαλλὲς τῆς ἱστορίας: 'something unlovely in the literal history', i.e. the letter seems harsh. Μαρία = Miriam (LXX spelling). Numbers 12:12 LXX reads κατεσθίει; Cyril has καταφάγεται; subject of 'it will eat away' is the disease, with 'her' most naturally Miriam. Numbers 19:11 (touching a corpse makes one unclean seven days) and 19:12 (purification on the third and seventh day) are cited as clear allusions to the law Cyril describes; the mourning relatives may also recall Numbers 19:14. 'God, who has power to give life to all things' may echo 1 Timothy 6:13 (τοῦ ζῳογονοῦντος τὰ πάντα); uncited as doubtful. Galatians 5:19–20: Cyril gives a shortened list (omits ἀσέλγεια, φαρμακεία and others; θυμοί placed before ζῆλοι). 'Passions of youth' (τοῖς εἰς νεότητα πάθεσι) may recall 2 Timothy 2:22; uncited as doubtful. Sense of κατεστιγμένον ('spotted all over') keeps the leprosy image. The section ends at Ἕτερός γε μήν; the sentence continues in section 4. In Numbers 12:11–12 it is Aaron who says 'Let her not become like a stillborn child'; Cyril's 'for he said' attributes the words to Moses. The English follows Cyril.

title: Discharge and corpse uncleanness read spiritually; Deuteronomy's exclusions
english: Cyril: …that is, the man with a discharge, signifies the one who lives always and without restraint in defilements, and wastes for nothing his nature’s aptitude for bearing virtuous and admirable fruit.
Palladius: Such as what?

Cyril: There is a great deal to say on all of this; but for now I will use one clear and most vivid example to show what I have said. Those who have a gifted mind, polished, so to speak, and who apply it to the teaching about the truth, will they not reap the beauty of right and exact doctrine as a fruit worth marveling at?
Palladius: Quite so.

Cyril: But those who have not chosen to think and do this, and instead turn their mind aside from the road it must take, and set it up as an advocate of unholy doctrines, or show it to be a servant of the wickedness that is in the world, make it a father of deceit and fraud. Losing to no useful end their nature’s aptitude for the good, they portray very well for us the man with a discharge, and show in their own ways a sickness of soul akin to the bodily affliction.
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: And the one unclean through the dead surely signifies the one who has shared in the deadness of others, and who carelessly lets himself be filled with other people’s offenses. To such a one the divine David also said somewhere: ‘If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you took your share with the adulterer’ (Psalm 50:18). For just as doing what is not permitted harms and deadens both soul and mind, so does approving of those who do such things; and the one who consents would be a partner with those who commit the sin themselves, for he is in no way blameless. That is why Paul too says: ‘Keep yourself pure, and do not share in other people’s sins’ (1 Timothy 5:22). This, I think, is what it means to be defiled by a dead body in the spiritual sense.
Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: Very rightly, then, he commanded the leper, the man with a discharge, and the one unclean through the dead to go away from the congregation, not allowing those whose uncleanness is hard to wash away to be joined to the companies of the saints. ‘For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?’ he says (2 Corinthians 6:14–15).
Palladius: So it is dangerous, then, to go into the house of God with unwashed feet, as it were.

Cyril: Most dangerous indeed, if it is true that offending God does not go unpunished. In Deuteronomy he also shuts others out of the holy court, saying: ‘One who is crushed or cut off shall not enter the assembly of the Lord. One born of a prostitute shall not enter the assembly of the Lord. An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter the assembly of the Lord; even to the tenth generation he shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, and even forever, because they did not… (Deuteronomy 23:1–4)
translator_notes: Psalm 50:18 = LXX Psalm 49:18. 1 Timothy 5:22: Cyril reverses the order of the two clauses. 2 Corinthians 6:14–15: the first question is the second half of 6:14, the second is 6:15b. Deuteronomy 23:1–4 uses English verse numbers (LXX/Hebrew 23:2–5); the quotation runs on into section 5 (23:4–6), so the English leaves the quotation open at the break and cites the verses covered here. In the second long Cyril turn the masculine predicates (συνήγορον, ὑπουργόν, γεννήτορα) are taken to refer to the mind (νοῦς) from the previous turn, while τὴν τῆς φύσεως ἐπιτηδειότητα is the object of ζημιούμενοι; the English names 'their mind' to make this plain. 'Approving of those who do such things' (συνευδοκεῖν) may echo Romans 1:32; uncited as doubtful. The sentence 'Very rightly, then, he commanded…' ends with a question mark in Migne but has no negative; rendered as a statement. Its subject (the law or God) is unstated; 'he' keeps the ambiguity. συναγωγή rendered 'congregation'; ἐκκλησία in Deuteronomy rendered 'assembly'.

title: The crushed, the cut off, the Ammonite and the Moabite
english: Cyril: …meet you with bread and water on the way when you were coming out of Egypt, and because they hired Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia against you, to curse you. But the Lord your God would not listen to Balaam, and the Lord your God turned the curses into a blessing, because the Lord your God loved you. You shall not speak words of peace to them, or words for their good, all your days forever’ (Deuteronomy 23:4–6).
Palladius: I should like to learn who is to be understood by the crushed and the cut off, the Ammonite and the Moabite.

Cyril: Listen, then. Eunuchs are not made in one way only, not one, Palladius; there are said to be two ways, and so it has been found. Some are castrated, with the male parts torn away; others still have them, but crushed and wholly useless. And sometimes people cruelly and impiously have the part of the body that begets children cut off, and they are incapable of a man’s functions, even though by nature and age they are counted among men. Now the male parts are a symbol of manly courage. We must take the crushed man, then, to be the one who has not, so to speak, been wholly torn away in soul and mind, but rather keeps somehow within himself his courage for what is good, though it is shattered; and the man cut off to be the one who has thrown these away entirely and been deprived of what most befits men. And to love a courage that is not sound stands, as it were, under the same charge as not wishing to be brave at all.
Palladius: Such as what?

Cyril: Some have slumped into fleshly desires, letting go of the reins entirely, as it were, to passion, and they cast their mind, rotten and unmanly, before the pleasures of licentiousness. Others, again, admire self-control, and sometimes take up splendid efforts toward it, but they dread the struggle and, unable to bear the onslaught of pleasure, end in weakness. Will you not, then, rightly call the one who has wholly given up efforts toward courage cut off? And will you not think the one who has in mind the will to be brave, yet is not also able to achieve virtue, crushed, neatly recasting even the body’s afflictions as qualities of character, and taking what is perceived by the senses as an image of things grasped by the mind and more hidden?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: Along with these, the Ammonite and the Moabite were shut out too, as unholy and utterly loathsome, men who set upon the saints like lions and pour out the arrows of envy and spite on those who are held in good repute. The Ammonites would be a type of the heretics, who know no pity; the Moabites, of those still lying under the errors of idolatry and the wickedness of demons. For both are hateful to God, and both are sick with a kindred boldness, as it were, against the saints.
translator_notes: Deuteronomy 23:4–6 in English numbering (LXX/Hebrew 23:5–7); it completes the quotation begun at the end of section 4. Cyril's text switches between plural 'you' (ὑμῖν) and singular (σέ) as LXX does; the English 'you' covers both. Οὐ προσαγορεύσεις εἰρηνικὰ αὐτοῖς καὶ συμφέροντα αὐτοῖς follows the LXX ('speak peace … and what is to their advantage'), not the Hebrew 'seek their peace'. Wordplay: ἀνδρεία/ἀνδρία (courage, literally 'manliness') with ἀνδρίζεσθαι ('to play the man') carries the eunuch figure; rendered 'manly courage', 'courage', 'be brave'. ἀποτέμνονταί τινες may be middle (some cut off their own member) or passive; the English 'have … cut off' allows both. τὸ μὴ ὑγιῶς ἀνδρίζεσθαι φιλεῖν rendered 'to love a courage that is not sound'. θεοστυγεῖς may mean 'hateful to God' or 'God-hating' (as in Romans 1:30); rendered 'hateful to God'. 'Like brothers' (ἀδελφὸν ὥσπερ … τὸ θράσος) plays on Ammon and Moab being brothers, sons of Lot's daughters (Genesis 19:36–38); uncited as a pun, not an allusion to the verse. 'Like lions' carries no clear Scripture reference here; uncited.

title: Kinsmen who refused Israel passage, and the heretics
english: Palladius: I do not quite understand what you mean.

Cyril: You will understand very well, and before long. The Ammonites, being descended from Esau, were near kin and of one blood with the sons of Jacob, I mean Israel. Yet those from Esau somehow disregarded nature itself and were false to the bond of kinship; from then on they proved harsh and unbending toward those who were close to them and of their own blood, that is, toward Israel. For when Israel set out from the land of the Egyptians and was passing by the country of the Ammonites, he begged the man who lived there, as a brother, to let them pass or hurry through, and to pity them as people who had been wronged; but he would not give way. But why do I say this? He went further: he took up arms and even made war. And he would have done them terrible harm had Israel not turned aside at the word of God. The text runs this way: ‘And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, saying: Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that has come upon us. Our fathers went down into Egypt, and we lived as strangers in Egypt many days, and the Egyptians ill-treated us and our fathers. And we cried out to the Lord, and the Lord heard our voice, and he sent angels and brought us out of Egypt. And now we are at Kadesh, a city on the edge of your borders. We will pass through your land. We will not go through fields or through vineyards, nor will we drink water from your cisterns. We will travel by the King’s Highway; we will not turn aside to the right or to the left until we have passed your borders. And Edom said to him: You shall not pass through me. Otherwise I will come out to meet you in war’ (Numbers 20:14–18). And a little further on: ‘And Edom came out to meet him with a great host and with a strong hand. And Edom would not allow Israel to pass through his borders. And Israel turned away from him’ (Numbers 20:20–21). Is the point not now clear and plain?
Palladius: Not altogether.

Cyril: Do you not see that, though they were joined to Israel by the tie of kinship, they were shown by the events themselves to be without natural affection and hard of heart, no different from wild beasts? When they ought to have pitied them as brothers, toiling and sweating as they were, they marched out to lay them waste. That is why the law says: ‘They shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, because they did not meet you with bread and water when you were coming out of Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 23:3–4); that is, because they were so utterly without compassion and had strayed into the unholiness of savage ways. You can see that the heretics, both their peoples and their leaders, are like this toward us who have chosen to walk uprightly. For as far as knowing the one and only God, the Father, and accepting faith in the Son and the Spirit is concerned, though not wholly soundly, they have a false show of brotherhood with us, and their kinship is counterfeit in intent. Yet when we are under persecution they do not come to our aid; rather, they even…
translator_notes: Cyril calls the people of Numbers 20 'Ammonites' and derives them from Esau; Scripture names them Edom (Esau's line), and the Ammonites came from Lot. The text is translated as written, keeping 'Ammonites' where Cyril uses it and 'Edom' inside the quotation. Numbers 20:16: Cyril's text reads plural ἀγγέλους ('he sent angels'); Rahlfs LXX has the singular. The Deuteronomy quotation is LXX Deuteronomy 23:4–5 (English 23:3–4); Scripture applies it to the Ammonite and Moabite, while Cyril applies it to his 'Ammonites' (Edom). The singular 'the man who lived there' (τὸν οἰκήτορα) and 'he' are kept as in the Greek. 'Walk uprightly' (ὀρθοποδεῖν) may echo Galatians 2:14 but is too faint for a citation. 'Show of brotherhood' renders δόξαν (opinion/repute) οὐκ ἀληθῆ. νοθηφοροῦσι γνώμῃ τὸ συγγενές is a rare word; rendered by sense, 'in their intent the kinship is counterfeit'. Section ends mid-sentence; the clause finishes in section 7.

title: Moab and Balaam; no greeting for heretics
english: Cyril: …load us further with wicked deeds of their own. ‘For they went out from us, but they were not of us,’ as it is written. ‘For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us’ (1 John 2:19). To these, whose gentleness is put on for show and who are not in the habit of doing what serves his glory, the Savior himself might very fittingly say: ‘Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters’ (Matthew 12:30). Do the workshops of the heretics, hateful to God, seem to you like the Ammonites, sick as they are beyond all bounds with a lack of compassion and of love for God?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: Now consider the Moabites too, if you like, who were openly the bitterest enemies of those who wish to serve the God who alone is God by nature and in truth. They were worshippers of idols, who put special trust in divinations and sorceries and were taken up beyond all measure with the flights of birds. Grinding their teeth at Israel’s good fortune, they hired Balaam and set him to curse; but by the inexpressible power of God the soothsayer’s mouth was turned to blessings they did not want (Numbers 22:5–6; Deuteronomy 23:4–5). Such would be the war that the pagans wage against us. They begrudge our Savior his glory and stir up all the strength of the devil against us; but divine grace from above shakes that strength down, pours feebleness over the herd of demons, and turns their way of plotting into something that brings gladness.
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: The holy places, then, are barred to the Ammonites and to the Moabites too, and very rightly. For those whose crimes are akin and whose boldness is of one kind may fittingly be caught in equal penalties. And see how careful the law is. It sets the saints wholly apart from them and charges them not even to wish so much as to enter into conversation with them, saying: ‘You shall not greet them in peace, and you shall not speak to them for their good, all your days for ever’ (Deuteronomy 23:6). Is this not plainly what that pair of saints, Paul and John, also taught us? One of them said: ‘If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not greet him’ (2 John 1:10); and this, I think, is ‘You shall not greet them in peace, nor for their good.’ The other, again: ‘After a first and a second warning, have nothing to do with a heretical man, knowing that such a person is perverted’ (Titus 3:10–11). This is ‘You shall not speak to them for their good.’ For the law says that we must give way to the utterly perverted as to madmen, and say to them: ‘Walk by the light of your fire, and by the flame that you have kindled’ (Isaiah 50:11). But the Ammonite is barred to the third generation, and the Moabite even to the tenth (Deuteronomy 23:3, 8); by the length of time, I think, God hints to us how great his indignation is against each. For the penalty of the heretics, as one would expect, is the lighter. For one might say…
translator_notes: Matthew 12:30 is word for word the same as Luke 11:23; Matthew is cited. The Balaam account is an allusion, not a quotation: the hiring is Numbers 22:5–6, and the curse turned to blessing is told in Deuteronomy 23:4–5 (LXX 23:5–6), the passage Cyril is expounding (compare Numbers 23:11; 24:10). The Moabite augury by 'flights of birds' has no specific verse; uncited. Deuteronomy 23:6 is LXX 23:7; the LXX reads προσαγορεύσεις εἰρηνικὰ αὐτοῖς καὶ συμφέροντα αὐτοῖς, and Cyril adds λαλήσεις so that he can split the verse into 'greet' (2 John) and 'speak for their good' (Titus); the English keeps that split. 'Paul and John' are named in that order, but 'the one' quotes 2 John 1:10 and 'the other' Titus 3:10–11; the English says 'one of them / the other' and lets the citations show who is who rather than adding names. Isaiah 50:11 is introduced by Cyril under 'the law' in the broad sense of Scripture; kept as written. Generations: Deuteronomy 23:3 bars Ammonite and Moabite to the tenth generation; the third-generation limit (23:8, LXX 23:9) belongs to the Edomite (and Egyptian). Cyril's 'Ammonite... to the third generation' follows from his calling Edom 'Ammonites' in section 6; both verses are cited. Ἕλληνες is rendered 'the pagans' (Greek idolaters, not ethnic Greeks), here and in section 8. Pronouns for God and Christ are lowercase per house style. Section ends mid-sentence ('For one might say'); the quotation follows in section 8.

title: No covenant with the nations; why the clean keep apart
english: Cyril: …of them too, just as of the Jews: ‘For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge’ (Romans 10:2). Thinking that they speak rightly and are wise, the wretches do not notice that they are fighting against the doctrines of the truth; and, mastered by a counterfeit zeal, they think that they are pleading the cause of God’s glory when they set themselves against those who walk uprightly. But the Moabites, that is, the ranks of the pagans, fight against the divine glory nakedly and openly, holding nothing back. That is why the law has hung a heavier penalty over them. Yet both are sent away from the sacred precincts as unholy and hateful to God.
Palladius: So it is no harmless thing, where defilement is concerned, to be fond of entering into talk with strangers and people of other beliefs, even if it goes no further than talk.

Cyril: You understand very well. That is why the law walls off from their foulness those who have been washed and are clean and who already belong to God, saying: ‘And it shall be, when the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to inherit, and you remove great and many and strong nations from before you, the Hittite and the Girgashite and the Amorite and the Canaanite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, seven nations many and great and stronger than you, and the Lord your God hands them over into your hands, and you strike them, you shall destroy them utterly. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor shall you show them mercy, nor shall you make marriages with them. You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son; for he will turn your son away from me, and he will serve other gods’ (Deuteronomy 7:1–4). So the law keeps us safe. ‘For you shall not make,’ it says, ‘a covenant with them’ (Deuteronomy 7:2). For what is still unholy cannot agree or be joined with what has been made holy, nor what is in mist and darkness with what has been enlightened, nor what is rejected with what has been received, nor what is thrust out of the holy and divine tabernacle with one who enters it.
Palladius: What, then, is the law guarding against? Why does it separate the clean so entirely from the unholy, even when someone is well established in virtue?

Cyril: Because the fear is very great, my friend, that even what seems to stand upright might somehow be shaken toward what it should not and be carried away from what is fitting, forced perhaps by someone, or by pleasure stirring it, or by the leaning toward this that is in our nature pushing it down into wrongdoing. For nature always leans somehow toward what is bad, and the divine word bears witness to us: ‘For the mind of man,’ it says, ‘is intently set on evil things from his youth’ (Genesis 8:21). If you wish, I will set before you as clear proof all that the daughter of Jacob is said to have suffered.
Palladius: You mean Dinah, I suppose; at least, I take it so.
Cyril: Certainly, Palladius. For this is written in the book of Genesis: ‘And there came…
translator_notes: Deuteronomy 7:1: Cyril's text reads ἐξαρεῖς ('you remove'); Rahlfs LXX has ἐξαρεῖ ('he removes'). The English follows Cyril. In 7:2 the quotation reads διαθήσῃ, and Cyril's repeat reads συνθήσῃ; both mean 'make a covenant'. Genesis 8:21 is quoted in the LXX form (ἐπιμελῶς ἔγκειται ἡ διάνοια); the verse number is the same in English Bibles. 'Nature always leans': the subject of ἀπονένευκε is supplied from φύσει in the clause before. 'Enlightened' (πεφωτισμένῳ) carries Cyril's usual baptismal sense; no citation. 'Pagans' renders Ἕλληνες, as in section 7. The Dinah quotation begins at the end of this section ('And there came') and finishes in section 9, where it is cited (Genesis 33:18–34:3).

title: Dinah leaves her father’s tent; David stays in God’s
english: Cyril: …Jacob to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, when he returned from Mesopotamia in Syria; and he camped facing the city. And he bought the piece of the field where he had pitched his tent from Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred lambs; and he set up an altar there and called upon the God of Israel. And Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to get to know the daughters of the people of the land; and Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the ruler of the land, saw her. And he took her and lay with her, and humbled her. And he set his heart on Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and he loved the young woman, and spoke to her in keeping with the young woman’s own mind’ (Genesis 33:18–20; 34:1–3). Notice, then, that while she still loved to stay in her father’s tent and lived there, where he had called upon the God of Israel and a holy altar had been raised, she was still undefiled and kept the glories of her virginity. But when she ran out of her father’s tent, and leaving the holy ground mingled with foreign women, she was at once forced into a defilement she had not known, and was no longer a virgin. At first she was subjected against her will to the pleasures of others; but afterwards she came to suffer this as well, that she wanted to be with the man who had taken advantage of her. For ‘he spoke to her,’ it says, ‘in keeping with the young woman’s own mind’ (Genesis 34:3).
Palladius: So it is.

Cyril: Then let us take what the senses perceive as an image of what the mind perceives, and say this: a soul that dwells in an excellent way of life, as in a kind of tent, will be wholly pure and clean and free from every foulness; but if it wanders off somewhere and hurries to the daughters of foreigners, that is, if it searches out and spies on the life of those in the world, its mind, gifted and noble as it is, will be corrupted. For to those whose aim is to live a shining life, spending their days with the wicked would do no small harm. But the divine David was never found wanting to go outside the holy tent; rather, he made it one of the chief things in his prayers to linger there and live close by, saying: ‘One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his holy temple. For he hid me in his tent in the day of my troubles; he sheltered me in the secret place of his tent’ (Psalm 27:4–5). By the divine and holy tent, I think, he means here the firm and unshaken state of a holy way of life; having, as it were, entered into it, he could not be taken by the passions that wished to ravage him.
Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: Well then, might one not learn more clearly and more truly that dealings with foreigners can sometimes bring defilements worse than any, even on those who are believed to stand firm, by bringing forward…
translator_notes: The Dinah quotation runs from Genesis 33:18 (begun at the end of section 8) to 34:3, skipping nothing between 33:20 and 34:1. LXX reads 'Salem, a city of Shechem/Shechemites' as a place name, and 'a hundred lambs' where the Hebrew has a hundred pieces of money; both kept as Cyril has them. Genesis 34:3 LXX ἐλάλησεν κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν τῆς παρθένου αὐτῇ (Hebrew 'spoke to the girl's heart') is rendered 'in keeping with the young woman's own mind', since Cyril's argument depends on that wording (she came to consent). 'Set his heart on' renders προσέσχε τῇ ψυχῇ. The Psalm is LXX Psalm 26:4–5, English Psalm 27:4–5; τερπνότης rendered 'delight'. 'Defilements worse than any' renders τὰ παντὸς ἐπέκεινα μολυσμοῦ. Section ends mid-sentence ('by bringing forward'); section 10 continues with Solomon's last years as the proof.

title: Solomon's fall through foreign wives
english: Cyril: …the end of Solomon’s life as proof, and what befell him on the very threshold of old age?
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: He was so brilliant and so celebrated that he had, in a sense, already won a glory beyond compare; yet he passed over into what is shameful, or rather he leapt down basely into the very depth of impiety toward God. His story runs like this. It is written in the Third Book of Kingdoms: ‘And Solomon grew greater than all the kings of the earth in wealth and in wisdom. And all the kings of the earth sought the face of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which the Lord had given in his heart’ (1 Kings 10:23–24). Yet this man, so glorious and so celebrated, who had advanced so far in wisdom that he became an object of boundless wonder even among the most eminent, was pried loose by pleasure in wicked women; and that pleasure, as it were, dragged him out of the divine tent itself and threw him into the pits of idolatry. For it is written of him: ‘And King Solomon was a lover of women, and he took foreign wives, and also the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Syrian, Hittite and Amorite women, from the nations about which the Lord had said to the sons of Israel, You shall not go in to them, and they shall not come in to you, lest they turn your hearts aside after their idols. To these Solomon clung in love. And he had seven hundred wives who were princesses, and three hundred concubines. And it came to pass in the time of Solomon’s old age that the foreign wives turned his heart aside after other gods. And his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father. And Solomon went after Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians, and after their king, the idol of the sons of Ammon. And Solomon did evil in the sight of the Lord, and did not follow the Lord as David his father did’ (1 Kings 11:1–6).

Is it not right to lament over one who is said to have suffered such things? The man who raised that famous temple in Jerusalem, who asked for the wisdom that sits beside the divine thrones (Wisdom of Solomon 9:4), who was admired for his matchless understanding to the very ends of the earth beneath heaven, who shone like the morning star over cities and lands: overcome by shameful women and following after a most loathsome pleasure, he is found to have fallen into such folly that he utterly disregarded even piety toward God itself. Beyond dispute, then, it is dangerous to keep company with foreigners. And it is altogether terrible to be overcome by fleshly pleasure. Such a man is unclean and hateful to the all-pure God, and without virtue he may not enter the holy and divine tent. Nor could he even offer an acceptable sacrifice. For it is written in Deuteronomy: ‘There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel, and no fornicator among the sons of Israel; and there shall be no… (Deuteronomy 23:17)
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, completing Cyril's question begun at the end of §9 ('…if one brought forward…'); the §9 translator should end on that clause. 'The Third Book of Kingdoms' is the Septuagint title of 1 Kings; LXX 3 Kingdoms 10:23-24 and 11:1-6 match English 1 Kings 10:23-24 and 11:1-6 in numbering. In 11:5 the LXX reads 'their king' (τοῦ βασιλέως αὐτῶν) for Milcom/Molech; kept as 'their king, the idol of the sons of Ammon'. 'The wisdom that sits beside the divine thrones' echoes Wisdom of Solomon 9:4 (τὴν τῶν σῶν θρόνων πάρεδρον σοφίαν), Solomon's prayer, so cited. 'Like the morning star' (ἑωσφόρος) may glance at Isaiah 14:12 (the fallen morning star), but Cyril uses it as praise here; uncited. 'Among the most eminent' renders παρά γε τοῖς ἄγαν διωρισμένοις (could also be 'the most discerning'). 'Without virtue he may not enter the holy and divine tent' renders the elliptical καὶ οὐκ ἀρετῆς δίχα … εἰσελάσαι σκηνήν (an implied 'it is possible'). γύναια is contemptuous ('wretched women'); rendered 'wicked women' with πονηρῶν. The Deuteronomy quotation runs over into §11; citation given at the break. LXX Deuteronomy 23:18 = English 23:17. Reviewer: 'and without virtue he may not enter' keeps ὁ τοιόσδε as the implied subject of the elliptical οὐκ ἀρετῆς δίχα … εἰσελάσαι (earlier draft generalised to 'no one'). ἀπεῖπε in the 1 Kings 11:2 quotation rendered 'had said to' (NETS 'about which the Lord said'); the draft's 'had forbidden the sons of Israel' was ungrammatical.

title: The prostitute's wage and the price of a dog
english: Cyril: …woman who pays tribute among the daughters of Israel, and no man made to pay tribute among the sons of Israel. You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God for any vow, for both are an abomination to the Lord your God’ (Deuteronomy 23:17–18).
Palladius: How severe the law is, and how very profitable!

Cyril: Well said, Palladius; you understand it rightly. And I think you would be still more astonished if you noticed that, by firmly checking the easy slide into pleasures, the law sends the lewd and unbridled man away. For see how it lays its charge both on those who wish to practice shameful defilement willingly and by their own choice, and also on those who are in the habit of bringing others down into it as if by compulsion. By what it says must not be done, it makes them safer, and leaves them hard put to find any word that could serve for their defense. For the charges are no longer charges of ignorance; from now on the indictment is one of carelessness and an unsubmissive mind.
Palladius: What do you mean?
Cyril: Do not some people go into fornication of their own accord? And do not women and youths who are willing to hire themselves out sell their bloom to the lusts of others?
Palladius: Yes.

Cyril: And again, are there not some who are overcome by shameful gain, who hand over to anyone who wants them their own maidservants, or such males as they may happen to have bought, and so the wretches collect money? Of them the prophet says: ‘And they sold the girls for wine, and drank’ (Joel 3:3). For it is true that some sink to such depths of wickedness and impurity that they impiously dare at times to levy tribute even on shameful things like these.
Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: So, then, those commit fornication willingly who, though they stand clear of the evil themselves, then go to it of their own judgment; but those who ‘pay tribute’ would be the ones who pay dues to others as if under compulsion, and gather the wages of lewdness for those who have bought them.
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: The law, then, forbids the thing in every form. It declares unholy anyone convicted on this charge, shuts him out of the holy tent, and at once closes the divine altar to him, saying that his sacrifice will not be received and his vow will not be accepted. For it is true that vows paid from a prostitute’s hire are not pure (Proverbs 19:13, Septuagint). In the same way it makes the price of a dog hateful and most loathsome. By ‘dog’, I think, it means the man who is easily drawn into impurity and simply gives himself to anyone who approaches; and the ‘price of a dog’ is whatever may be offered to him in payment for himself. So let the law cry out: ‘There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel, and no fornicator among the sons of Israel’ (Deuteronomy 23:17). And let the most wise Paul sound in harmony with it, crying aloud: ‘Flee… (1 Corinthians 6:18)
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation, completing Deuteronomy 23 from §10. LXX Deuteronomy 23:18-19 = English 23:17-18 (the LXX has extra clauses on τελεσφόρος/τελισκόμενος). In the LXX these words most likely mean cult initiates (Hebrew qedeshah/qadesh), but Cyril explains τελεσφόροι as those who 'pay tribute' (φόρους τελοῦντες) to others under compulsion, that is, people prostituted by owners; the quotation is therefore rendered 'who pays tribute' / 'made to pay tribute' so his explanation reads correctly. ἄλλαγμα κυνός rendered 'the price of a dog' throughout, matching Cyril's gloss ('what is offered to him for himself'). Joel 3:3 English = LXX and Hebrew Joel 4:3. 'Vows paid from a prostitute's hire are not pure' (οὐχ ἁγναὶ εὐχαὶ ἀπὸ μισθώματος πόρνης) is the Septuagint plus at Proverbs 19:13 (εὐχαὶ ἀπὸ μισθώματος ἑταίρας οὐχ ἁγναί), not in the Hebrew or English Bible; cited with 'Septuagint' so readers are not sent to the wrong English verse. Doubtful reading: οἱ μέν, τὸ αὐτοὶ ἔξω φέρεσθαι τοῦ κακοῦ is obscure in the print (perhaps corrupt for τῷ αὐτοί …); see the reviewer note below. The εὐχή of Deuteronomy is a vow; kept as 'vow' in Cyril's comment. γραφή here is the legal 'indictment'. The Paul quotation runs over into §12. Reviewer: the obscure οἱ μέν, τὸ αὐτοὶ ἔξω φέρεσθαι τοῦ κακοῦ is now rendered 'though they stand clear of the evil themselves' (accusative of respect: under no compulsion toward it), keeping ἔξω ('outside'); the earlier 'carried off into the evil by their own doing' reversed ἔξω. The contrast willing vs compelled is secured by ἑκουσίως and ἰδιογνωμόνως either way. θύμα is 'sacrifice'; εὐχή stays 'vow'.

title: A living sacrifice, and Israel's sin at Peor
english: Cyril: …from fornication. Every sin that a man commits is outside the body, but the fornicator sins against his own body’ (1 Corinthians 6:18). And let him also call those who press nobly toward the glories of self-control to strive for what is better. For again he said: ‘I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and well pleasing to God, which is your reasonable worship. Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and well pleasing and perfect’ (Romans 12:1–2). Or would you deny that putting away shameful things is a sacrifice truly holy and wholly pure?
Palladius: I would certainly say it is; how could it not be?

Cyril: When we turn away from fleshly pleasure, God rejoices over us; but he looks with deep displeasure on those who turn aside to weakness, and on those who have chosen to fall in behind the flesh he brings punishment. For hot and unbridled pleasure sometimes forces a man even into apostasy from God. That this is true, the account of Solomon would show at once. But before him Israel is found to have been led astray into this very thing in the wilderness. For it is written: ‘Israel encamped at Shittim, and the people profaned themselves by committing fornication with the daughters of Moab. And they invited them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices and worshipped their idols. And Israel was initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor, and the Lord was angry with Israel in his wrath. And the Lord said to Moses: Take all the chiefs of the people and make an example of them before the Lord in the face of the sun, and the fierce anger of the Lord will turn away from Israel’ (Numbers 25:1–4).

Do you see how the divine and most gentle nature is somehow provoked by us, and all but driven into an anger it does not desire? For it is a thing fit for beasts, I mean going mad over the beauty of women; and it is utterly unholy as well to dare to give up piety toward God in exchange for unbridled pleasure. That is why they are made an example before the Lord in the face of the sun: that is, they were hung on upright stakes turned toward the east, and this was the manner of their punishment. The type all but cries out plainly and raises its voice to say that no one caught in such sins will escape the all-seeing eye of the Judge, which cannot be deceived, nor will he get away unpunished; rather, as the prophet’s word says, he will be set out ‘as a spectacle to all flesh’ (Isaiah 66:24), paying the bitter penalty for his offenses.
Palladius: So by ‘in the face of the sun’ it means being punished openly, and being made an example, as it were, before the eyes of God.

Cyril: Quite so; and our reading is not wide of the mark. And that those who commit fornication, or who have been prostituted, must give account to God for so cold and profane a life, and that hidden things are laid bare…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation, completing 1 Corinthians 6:18 from §11. λογικὴ λατρεία rendered 'reasonable worship' to keep the link with the work's theme of worship (λατρεία). 'Shittim' is the LXX Σαττείν; 'Baal of Peor' is Βεελφεγώρ; ἐτελέσθη ('was initiated') kept rather than the English 'yoked himself'. Cyril's 'hung on upright stakes turned toward the east' is his own explanation of 'in the face of the sun'; he draws no cross typology here, so none is added. 'As a spectacle to all flesh' (εἰς ὅρασιν πάσῃ σαρκί) is the LXX of Isaiah 66:24 (English 'an abhorrence to all flesh'). πρὸς Θεὸν οἱ λόγοι ('must give account to God') may echo Hebrews 4:13 (πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος), and 'hidden things are laid bare' may echo 1 Corinthians 4:5 or Luke 8:17; both too loose to cite. The section ends mid-sentence; the main verb ('this is sketched out … through another law') follows in §13. The previous English wrongly placed '(Numbers 25:1–4)' at the end of this section's last turn; the citation now stands beside the Numbers quotation. Reviewer: τῆς εὐσεβείας ἄλλαγμα ποιεῖσθαι τὴν ἡδονήν = to make pleasure the price paid for piety, i.e. to give up piety for pleasure; reworded so the trade runs the right way in English. πεπορνευμένοις rendered 'who have been prostituted', matching Cyril's earlier distinction between willing fornicators and those prostituted by others (τελισκόμενος).

title: The law of the wife suspected of adultery
english: Cyril: …and what is in each person will be clearly known, this is sketched out for us again through another law. For it is written in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: If any man’s wife goes astray and wholly disregards him, and a man lies with her carnally, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she conceals it, and she is defiled, and there was no witness against her, and she was not caught in the act; and a spirit of jealousy comes upon him, and he is jealous of his wife, and she has been defiled; or a spirit of jealousy comes upon him, and he is jealous of his wife, and she has not been defiled: then the man shall bring his wife to the priest, and shall bring the offering for her, a tenth of an ephah of barley meal. He shall not pour oil on it, nor put frankincense on it, for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, a sacrifice of remembrance, which brings sin to remembrance. And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the Lord. And the priest shall take pure living water in an earthen vessel, and some of the earth that is on the floor of the tent of witness, and the priest shall take it and cast it into the water. And the priest shall set the woman before the Lord, and uncover the woman’s head, and put into her hands the sacrifice of remembrance, the sacrifice of jealousy; and in the priest’s hand shall be the water of conviction that brings this curse. And the priest shall put her under oath and say to the woman: If no man has lain with you, if you have not gone astray to be defiled while under your own husband, be free from this water of conviction that brings the curse. But if you have gone astray while under a husband, if you have been defiled, and some man other than your husband has lain with you… then the priest shall put the woman under the oaths of this curse, and the priest shall say to the woman: May the Lord make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the Lord makes your thigh fall away and your belly swell. And this water that brings the curse shall enter your belly, to make your womb swell and your thigh fall away. And the woman shall say: So be it, so be it. And the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of conviction that brings the curse, and he shall make the woman drink the water of conviction that brings the curse. And the water of conviction that brings the curse shall enter into her. And the priest shall take the sacrifice of jealousy from the woman’s hand, and lay the sacrifice before the Lord, and bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take a handful from the sacrifice as its memorial portion and offer it up on the altar, and after this he shall make the woman drink the water. And it shall be, if she has been defiled and has escaped her husband’s notice, that the water of conviction that brings the curse shall enter into her, and her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall be a curse among her people. But if she has not been defiled… (Numbers 5:11–28)
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing the clause that ends §12 ('…and that hidden things are laid bare'); the main verb διετύπου ('sketched out', 'outlined in figure') has no named subject; it could be God as lawgiver or Moses (see the reviewer note below). The whole section is the LXX of Numbers 5:11-28, ending mid-verse 28; ἡ γυνή ('the woman') stands at the head of §14, so §13 ends 'But if she has not been defiled…' and the §14 translator should continue '…and is clean, she shall be free…' without repeating 'the woman'. LXX differences kept: 'pure living water' (ὕδωρ καθαρὸν ζῶν; Hebrew 'holy water'; 'living' kept because Cyril reads it of Christ in §14–15, where he cites it as 'living and pure'), 'uncover the woman's head', 'water of conviction' (ἐλεγμός; English 'water of bitterness'), and verse 20's broken construction (marked with an ellipsis before 'then the priest'). οἰφί is the ephah. The print doubles the verb in verse 27 (λήθῃ λάθῃ, an OCR or typesetting duplicate); translated once. 'Tent of witness' is the LXX name for the tabernacle (σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου). Reviewer: διετύπου has no expressed subject; rendered impersonally ('this is sketched out for us') rather than 'He', so the English does not decide between God and Moses where the Greek does not.

title: The suspected wife and the judgment seat of Christ
english: Cyril: ‘…and is clean, she shall be free of guilt and shall conceive offspring.’ (Numbers 5:28) That is what the law says. And I would say that the divine Paul, gathering very aptly into a few thoughts what is set out at length in these writings, writes to us: ‘For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive back what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad.’ (2 Corinthians 5:10)
Palladius: I think that is rightly said. But explain carefully each point of what has been decreed.

Cyril: He commanded that the woman suspected of adultery, when she faces a charge that has no proofs, be brought to the priest and stand in the sight of God (Numbers 5:15–16); and this, I think, means that all are going to stand before Christ (Romans 14:10). Next, he commanded that the gift offered for her be barley meal, not sprinkled with frankincense, not moistened with oil; for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, which brings sin to remembrance (Numbers 5:15). It is plain, then, that from each person’s life a kind of odor, as it were, rises up to God: against those who have let themselves slide into carelessness it brings the charge of every monstrous deed, but for those who have striven earnestly to live rightly and well it bears witness to their genuineness. That is why we say, and with very good reason, that the gifts of those who are not under suspicion consist of fine wheat flour, with frankincense added and oil poured over it (Leviticus 2:1). For it will surely follow that a life which stays human, of which the fine wheat flour would also be a type, must be reckoned as fragrance and gladness before God, who loves virtue. But barley meal would be a very clear sign of a spurious and beastlike life. For to be unrestrained in appetite, and to want to rush without a bridle into monstrous pleasures, is somehow more fitting for cattle, and not at all becoming to a human being. That is why the woman accused of a spurious life brought barley meal to God without frankincense and oil, that is, without fragrance and gladness; for it is a sacrifice that brings sin to remembrance. And where sin is brought to remembrance, how or from where could gladness come? For the one on trial is not in hope of crowns, but in fear of punishment and fire. Besides this, the woman is brought to the judge with her head uncovered (Numbers 5:18), that is, not in her usual and fitting adornment. And what would be the reason for this? The charges are of unseemliness, and the indictment is for shameless conduct. Remember that Paul, who was learned in the law, does not allow a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered (1 Corinthians 11:5), and takes the law of nature (1 Corinthians 11:14) as his proof that she must be covered: ‘For her hair,’ he says, ‘is given to her as a covering.’ (1 Corinthians 11:15) So the woman, accused of unseemliness, was no longer in seemly adornment. But she is uncovered in another sense too. For all things are naked before the eyes of the Judge (Hebrews 4:13), and no one at all could escape the notice of him who searches hearts and inward parts (Psalm 7:9), who also says through the voice of the prophet: ‘I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?’ (Jeremiah 23:23–24) Yet the law hints again, in a riddle, that Christ is the one who judges. For it said that living and…
translator_notes: PG 68.912. Opens mid-sentence inside the Numbers 5:11–28 quotation begun in §13; ἡ γυνή (the subject of §13’s closing ‘Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ μιανθῇ’) is the first word here, so the English starts ‘…and is clean’ to join §13’s ‘But if she has not been defiled…’. Cited (Numbers 5:28) because §13 already carries (Numbers 5:11–28) at its break. OCR: ‘ὀλίγαι·’ read as ὀλίγαις; ‘κομίσται’ read as κομίσηται (2 Corinthians 5:10). Cyril’s 2 Corinthians 5:10 has plural ἀγαθά/φαῦλα where NA has singular; sense unchanged. Romans 14:10 cited for ‘all are going to stand before Christ’ because Cyril uses the same verb (παραστήσεσθαι; Romans 14:10 πάντες γὰρ παραστησόμεθα τῷ βήματι); some witnesses there read ‘of Christ’. Leviticus 2:1 is the grain offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense that Cyril contrasts with Numbers 5:15. ἐρήμην … γραφήν: a legal phrase, here ‘a charge without proofs’ (ἐλέγχων), matching Numbers 5:13 ‘no witness’. τῇ τέως ἀνθρωπίνῃ ζωῇ: τέως taken as ‘still, so far’ (a life that stays human, against the beastlike life that follows); rendered ‘a life which stays human’. νόθος / γνήσιον: rendered ‘spurious’ / ‘genuineness’ to keep Cyril’s pair (the words also mean illegitimate/legitimate birth, apt for an adultery case). κόσμος / ἀκοσμία wordplay rendered ‘adornment … unseemliness … seemly adornment’. 1 Corinthians 11:15: Cyril has κόμη … ἀντὶ περιβολαίου δέδοται αὐτῇ, NA word order differs; the ‘law of nature’ alludes to 1 Corinthians 11:14 (‘Does not nature itself teach you’), cited by the reviewer as a clear allusion. Hebrews 4:13 (γυμνὰ … τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς) is a clear verbal allusion. ‘Searches hearts and kidneys’: LXX Psalm 7:10 (= English Psalm 7:9) ἐτάζων καρδίας καὶ νεφρούς; the same phrase is in Jeremiah 17:10 and 11:20; cited to the Psalm, whose wording (ἐτάζων) Cyril matches; νεφροί rendered ‘inward parts’. Jeremiah 23:23 is quoted from the LXX; ‘Shall anything be hidden from me?’ is Cyril’s short form of 23:24 (LXX: εἰ κρυβήσεταί τις ἐν κρυφαίοις, καὶ ἐγὼ οὐκ ὄψομαι αὐτόν;). Uncited: oil as gladness (cf. Psalm 45:7 ‘oil of gladness’), not a clear allusion here. Terms kept consistent with §13 (chunk 2): ‘barley meal’, ‘earthen vessel’, ‘brings sin to remembrance’. Note for the joiner: §13’s quotation renders ὕδωρ καθαρὸν ζῶν as ‘pure running water’; Cyril’s reading in §15 rests on ζῶν = ‘living’ (the life-giving Word), so here and in §15 it is ‘living and pure water’; consider ‘pure living water’ in §13 too. Section ends mid-sentence (καθα|ρόν).

title: The living water in the earthen vessel: the Word made flesh
english: Cyril: …pure water must be poured into an earthen vessel, together with some of the earth that lies in the tent (Numbers 5:17). Then, when the words of the curse had been washed off into the water, he commanded the woman suspected of fornication to drink it (Numbers 5:23–24). And he says: ‘If she is guilty of the charge, her belly will swell and her thigh will fall away; but if she is clear of the accusation, and what was suspected of her is not true, she will conceive offspring.’ (Numbers 5:27–28)
Palladius: What, then, is the meaning? Or how would Christ be signified to us even through the things just named?

Cyril: By the living and pure water you will understand the life-giving Word of God, who is truly pure and has no share in sin at all, and who came to be in flesh as in an earthen vessel. For how, or on what ground, could anyone doubt that the flesh is dust and comes from the earth? By the earth from the tent you will understand him who was in death for our sake; for it was said to human nature: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall return.’ (Genesis 3:19) And by the words of the curse you will understand very well him who became a curse for us by being hung on a tree (Galatians 3:13). For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.’ (Galatians 3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23) So when Emmanuel, who is God by nature, reaches down into the depth of the human mind, he will convict and punish those who are guilty of sins; but those who are not caught in them he will show to be fruitful. For this, I think, is the meaning of ‘she will conceive offspring’: the bodily experience signifies the fruitfulness of the soul.
Palladius: Excellently said.

Cyril: Fornication, then, and the passions of the flesh debase a person and drive him out of his closeness to God; for ‘those who are in the flesh cannot please God.’ (Romans 8:8) By ‘flesh,’ as I take it, he means the mind set on the flesh (Romans 8:6–7); for that is how the text would rightly be understood. And besides this, a wicked disposition, a savage cast of character, and a drift into anything whatever of the most monstrous kind make us loathsome and unholy. For it befits us not only to master the passions of the flesh, but also to excel in gentleness of character, to show ourselves above all diligent in love toward the brothers, to be seen crowned with the glories of righteousness, and besides this to keep within ourselves a mind that is keen and well trained, that approaches the teachings about God without distortion, and that in searching into doctrines keeps what is blameless at every point. For such people are perfect, since in truth they lack none of the highest goods. The divine Paul also told us that the man of God must be complete (2 Timothy 3:17); and by ‘complete’ he means one who is equipped for every good work and well fitted to achieve virtue fully. Or is it not so?
Palladius: How could it not be?
Cyril: See, then, how the law, speaking in riddles,…
translator_notes: PG 68.913. Opens mid-word (καθα|ρόν) completing §14’s ‘For it said that living and…’. ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς: Cyril’s short form of Numbers 5:17 ‘the earth on the floor of the tent’; rendered ‘the earth that lies in the tent’. The ‘quotation’ ‘If she is guilty… she will conceive offspring’ is Cyril’s paraphrase of Numbers 5:27–28, not the LXX wording; it is kept in quotation marks as the print has it. Genesis 3:19 LXX: γῆ εἶ καὶ εἰς γῆν ἀπελεύσῃ, quoted exactly. Galatians 3:13 quoted exactly (ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου); Paul there quotes Deuteronomy 21:23 (LXX κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ θεοῦ), so both are cited. Romans 8:8 quoted exactly. ‘The fleshly mind’ (σαρκικὸν φρόνημα) echoes Romans 8:6–7 (τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός), cited as a clear allusion. 2 Timothy 3:17: Cyril’s ἐξηρτυμένον for NA ἐξηρτισμένος; sense the same. The earthen vessel for Christ’s flesh may echo 2 Corinthians 4:7 (ἐν ὀστρακίνοις σκεύεσιν) and ‘dust … from the earth’ Genesis 2:7; both doubtful, uncited. ‘Emmanuel’ is the title from Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23, used as a name, not quoted; uncited. καθίκοιτο εἰς … βάθος: ‘reaches down into the depth’, mirroring the water entering the woman’s belly. ἐλέγξει κολάζων rendered ‘convict and punish’. ἐξιτηλία is rare (from ἐξίτηλος, ‘fading, lapsing’); rendered ‘a drift into’; the sense (a sliding away into every vice) is clear from context, the exact nuance uncertain. ‘Brothers’ for ἀδελφούς (fellow believers). The section ends mid-sentence; the law is the subject of the participle and main verb that follow in §16 (παρενεγκὼν … ὀνίνησι).

title: Scripture teaches through animals, plants and stones; the clean and unclean beasts
english: Cyril: …brings in many irrational animals, and kinds of birds and water creatures as well, to sketch human characters, and so benefits us in countless ways. And do not be surprised at this, since at times it likens us even to plants, using the natural quality of each to mark out neatly what belongs to each of us. For God said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, hinting at the fragrance of those who through faith in Christ have blossomed anew into life (a spiritual fragrance, clearly), and at the heights they reach in virtue: ‘And I will make living water in the desert, and rivers in a waterless land’ (Isaiah 43:19–20), ‘and I will set in the waterless land the cedar and the box tree, the myrtle, the cypress and the white poplar.’ (Isaiah 41:19) And again: ‘And it shall be,’ he says, ‘that instead of the scrub a cypress shall come up, and instead of the fleabane a myrtle shall come up.’ (Isaiah 55:13) By scrub and fleabane, I think, he aptly names souls still untamed, which appear in the eyes of the Godhead like wild thorn. And at times the venerable company of the saints is also likened to stones: ‘For holy stones are rolling on the earth.’ (Zechariah 9:16) And the Savior, too, said that the kingdom of heaven is like leaven and like a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 13:31–33). So it is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture to make human things plain through many very vivid examples.
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: Observe, then, that Scripture, bringing forward to good purpose countless kinds of beasts, and of birds and swimming creatures too, brands some as unclean and wholly defiled, and accepts others again and clears them of reproach, so that those who serve God may rightly know what conduct would keep them from being accepted, and by wisely abstaining from what they will be far from blame and will shine, worthy of acceptance and honored by the verdict from above. The law on this matter runs as follows: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say: These are the animals that you shall eat out of all the animals on the earth. Every animal that parts the hoof and is cloven-footed with two claws, and brings up the cud, among the animals, these you shall eat. But of these you shall not eat, of those that bring up the cud and of those that part the hoof and are cloven-footed: the camel, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof; it is unclean to you. And the hare, because it brings up the cud and does not part the hoof; it is unclean to you. And the rock badger, because it brings up the cud and does not part the hoof; it is unclean to you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed, but does not bring up the cud; it is unclean to you. You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall not eat of their carcasses; they are unclean to you.’ (Leviticus 11:1–8) Now Christ says most plainly: ‘It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person.’ (Matthew 15:11) And somewhere it was also said to the inspired Peter, when the sheet was let down from above by its four corners (Acts 10:11–12), in which, it is written, were all the…
translator_notes: PG 68.916. Opens mid-sentence: §15 ends ‘Θέα δὴ οὖν ὅπως αἰνιγματωδῶς ὁ νόμος εἰς’ and the law (masc. παρενεγκών) is the subject of ὀνίνησι here; the English splits as ‘See, then, how the law, speaking in riddles,…’ / ‘…brings in … and so benefits us’. The first Isaiah quotation is a conflation: ‘I will make in the desert … in a waterless land rivers’ matches Isaiah 43:19 LXX (ποιήσω ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ὁδὸν καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀνύδρῳ ποταμούς), where Cyril has ‘living water’ for ‘a way’, the ‘water’ coming from 43:20 LXX (ἔδωκα ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ὕδωρ καὶ ποταμοὺς ἐν τῇ ἀνύδρῳ), so cited 43:19–20; the tree list matches Isaiah 41:19 LXX exactly (θήσω εἰς τὴν ἄνυδρον γῆν κέδρον καὶ πύξον καὶ μυρσίνην καὶ κυπάρισσον καὶ λεύκην). Both are cited beside their clauses. Isaiah 55:13 LXX quoted (στοιβή ‘brushwood, thorny scrub’; κόνυζα ‘fleabane’, a rank-smelling weed; English Bibles from the Hebrew have ‘thorn’ and ‘brier’). Zechariah 9:16 LXX (λίθοι ἅγιοι κυλίονται ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς αὐτοῦ; Cyril drops αὐτοῦ); the Hebrew differs (‘jewels of a crown’). Matthew 13:31–33 (mustard seed and leaven; Luke 13:18–21 is parallel). Leviticus 11:1–8 LXX quoted with Cyril’s variants: his text has ‘you shall not eat of their carcasses’ where the LXX has ‘you shall not touch’ (οὐχ ἅψεσθε); rendered as he has it. The hare stands before the rock badger, as in the LXX order; the Hebrew and English Bibles put the rock badger first (Leviticus 11:5) and the hare second (11:6). ὀνυχιστῆρας ὀνυχίζον δύο χηλῶν rendered ‘is cloven-footed with two claws’; μηρυκισμὸν ἀνάγει kept literal as ‘brings up the cud’ because §18’s reading depends on bringing food up from the belly. Matthew 15:11 quoted in short form (NA: οὐ τὸ εἰσερχόμενον εἰς τὸ στόμα κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον). Acts 10:11–12 summarised (the sheet by four corners); quotation of Acts 10:13 follows in §17. ἐν ᾗ πάντα γέγραπται: γέγραπται likely ‘it is written’ (in Acts) rather than ‘depicted’; taken so. Scripture (feminine participle παρενεγκοῦσα) is the subject of the third Cyril turn. θεόπνευστος echoes 2 Timothy 3:16 as a word only; uncited. ‘The Godhead’ for ἡ θεότης.

title: The law defiles nothing: animals as pictures of character; righteousness is twofold
english: Cyril: …four-footed animals and birds: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ (Acts 10:13) When the disciple cried out, still fearing the observance of the law, and said, ‘By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean, nor has any profane meat entered my mouth’ (Acts 10:14; Acts 11:8), God spoke again: ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call common.’ (Acts 10:15) And the inspired Paul also writes that ‘food does not commend us to God.’ (1 Corinthians 8:8) It is quite clear, then, that the law by no means makes anything that exists profane, but knows that all things are pure to the pure (Titus 1:15). Rather, by taking the natural traits of each animal very aptly as pictures of the qualities of human character, it does no small good. And you could learn from the following, too, that what I say is true and beyond doubt. For he is seen to command that things condemned by everyone must be abhorred: I mean the camel and the rock badger, the night raven and the cormorant, the gecko and the shrew, and things still more shameful than these (Leviticus 11:4–5; Leviticus 11:17; Leviticus 11:30). Would not the lawgiver’s aim be plain, then, at least in these cases, my good friend?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: So we must aptly carry over to the quality of character the traits that are naturally present in certain irrational animals, each animal, so to speak, depicting in itself the ways of a certain kind of person and indicating what traits he has. For are we not ourselves accustomed, in a way, to call those who are very hot-blooded and very strong, and who surpass others in boldness, boars or lions or something else of that kind; and to call those who are gentle and quiet, and whose minds are humble, sheep and doves, and sometimes to crown them with the name ‘calm’, giving to each person’s ways the fitting description drawn from things more easily seen?
Palladius: True.
Cyril: Let us go on, then, to the aim of the law, and inquire carefully into what it is that it enjoins.
Palladius: Let us go on.

Cyril: The glories of righteousness, and in a word of all goodness, spring perhaps from each person’s own choice; yet they are achieved, I think, in two ways, and in a sense they have a twofold outworking.
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: Either we do some good to ourselves: cutting away monstrous and blameworthy pleasures, putting to death our members that are on earth (Colossians 3:5), settling the mind in gentleness of spirit, practicing poverty, and keeping our thinking as pure and untroubled as we can; or else we fulfill our good endeavors toward our brothers: showing no malice to those who choose to grieve us and who have heartlessly offended us, helping the weary, comforting those who grieve, turning those who have strayed through ignorance back to what is right, leading them by the hand toward what is better…
translator_notes: PG 68.917. Opens mid-sentence, completing §16’s ‘in which, it is written, were all the…’. Acts 10:13 quoted (θῦσον ‘kill’, as in English Bibles). Peter’s reply blends Acts 10:14 (οὐδέποτε ἔφαγον πᾶν κοινὸν καὶ ἀκάθαρτον) with the retelling in Acts 11:8 (οὐδέποτε εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ στόμα μου); Cyril has κρέας βέβηλον, ‘profane meat’, a phrase in neither verse; both verses cited. Acts 10:15 quoted (also Acts 11:9). 1 Corinthians 8:8: Cyril’s present παρίστησι for NA future παραστήσει; rendered in Cyril’s present tense, ‘does not commend us to God’. Titus 1:15 (πάντα καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς) is a clear verbal allusion. The list of unclean creatures gathers Leviticus 11 by its LXX names: camel (11:4), rock badger χοιρογρύλλιος (English 11:5; LXX order 11:6), νυκτικόραξ ‘night raven’ and καταρράκτης ‘cormorant’ (11:17 LXX; English Bibles from the Hebrew have ‘little owl’ and ‘cormorant’), ἀσκαλαβώτης ‘gecko’ (LXX 11:30 καλαβώτης, Cyril’s spelling ἀσκαλαβώτης is the classical form) and μυγαλῆ ‘shrew’ (11:30). προστεταχὼς … λέγων: the subject is ‘he’, the lawgiver named in the next sentence. τῷ τῇ γαλήνης ὀνόματι: print error for τῷ τῆς γαλήνης ὀνόματι; ‘the name of calm’, i.e. calling such people ‘calm’; doubtful whether a pun on an animal name is meant, none assumed. σῦς rendered ‘boars’ (θερμοί, bold, strong). γνώμη ‘choice’; ἐπιείκεια ‘goodness’. διφυᾶ … τὴν ἔκφασιν: ἔκφασις (‘expression’) may be a misprint for ἔκβασις (‘outcome’); ‘outworking’ covers both. ἤγουν normally ‘that is’, but here it introduces the second of the two ways promised (ἢ … ἤγουν), so ‘or else’. ἐν πνεύματι rendered ‘gentleness of spirit’ (lower case); it may mean the Holy Spirit (cf. Galatians 5:23; 6:1), doubtful, uncited. πτωχείαν ἐπιτηδεύοντες: ‘practicing poverty’ (voluntary poverty; possible echo of Matthew 5:3, uncited). Colossians 3:5 (νεκρώσατε … τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) is a clear verbal allusion. κάμνοντες ‘the weary’ (also ‘the sick’). The list continues into §18 (ἐπαρκοῦντες δεομένοις…); the English ends with an ellipsis.

title: The parted hoof and the chewed cud
english: Cyril: …coming to the aid of those in need, and taking great pains to carry out whatever things God delights in. Is not the way of righteousness, then, in a sense twofold, since it is carried out both toward ourselves and toward others?
Palladius: It seems so.

Cyril: The law, then, always likens such a person, in a way, to a parted hoof, that is, to a foot divided in two (Leviticus 11:3). For the foot would always be for us a symbol and type of the road we travel in practical action. Indeed we speak of those who are truly eager to go blamelessly toward what leads to their good as walking with a straight foot. David also sings somewhere: ‘For my foot has stood on level ground’ (Psalm 26:12), that is, I have walked in righteousness and uprightness, and I have hated what is crooked. And of those who love sin he says: ‘Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery are in their paths’ (Romans 3:15–16). So the foot is a symbol of the road we travel in deeds. And the parting of the hoof would be a clear type of our being able to walk rightly and beyond reproach in both ways: in what concerns ourselves, and also toward others.
Palladius: The argument is persuasive.

Cyril: Suppose, then, there is someone who knows how to walk rightly and skillfully in both ways, and is able to benefit both himself and others (I mean by the quality of his character). Suppose that besides this he is sensible and very wise, and gives his heart to the words about God as a kind of lodging and dwelling place; that he is always turning over within himself, this way and that, the meanings of the divine doctrines, and so knows how to search them out often and wisely, grinding fine, as it were, the thoughts he has come to know so exactly. Such a person will surely resemble an animal that brings up the cud: it is always bringing back up the food in its belly and putting it under its teeth, so that it may be ground finer still and, made fine enough to digest, may turn to its benefit.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: Now the law says that an animal is clean if its foot ends in a parted hoof and it also brings back up the cud from its belly (Leviticus 11:3). For the one who is by nature excellent and good toward himself and toward others, and who has also taken on a love of learning and practice in knowledge (plainly, the knowledge of God), will be fully fitted for virtue and for every admirable thing, and blameless, at least in what concerns himself. And if someone comes to share in such a person (I mean by learning from him), and feasts, as it were, on the teaching he gives; if he becomes his imitator and chooses to emulate one so distinguished and outstanding, he will be undefiled and clean. For he will be living with one who is clean, and he will at once show his own way of life to be a kind of imprint of the understanding and sound learning found in that man. This, I think, is what is meant by our having to eat of every animal that by nature splits its foot at the hoof and brings up…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing Cyril's list of good works done toward others begun at the end of §17 (the §17 English should end on that list). 'For my foot has stood on level ground' is LXX Psalm 25:12, English Psalm 26:12 (εὐθύτης, 'uprightness' or 'level ground'). 'Their feet are swift to shed blood…' matches Romans 3:15–16 word for word (ὀξεῖς); Paul draws it from Isaiah 59:7–8, and some LXX manuscripts carry the same lines in Psalm 13:3 (English 14:3); Cyril's 'of those who love sin' may still be David speaking, but the wording follows Romans, so Romans is cited. The gloss 'I have hated what is crooked' is Cyril's own paraphrase, not cited. 'Walk with a straight foot' (ὀρθῷ ποδί) is a common Greek proverb, not Scripture; compare Galatians 2:14 (ὀρθοποδοῦσιν), uncited. 'Fully fitted… for every admirable thing' (ἄρτιος… πρὸς πᾶν) may echo 2 Timothy 3:17; doubtful, uncited. The infinitive ἐξερευνᾷν is taken as governed by εἰδώς ('knows how to search them out'). The section breaks inside a word, ἀνάνον|τος (§19); read ἀνάγοντος, the Leviticus 11:3 verb (ἀνάγον μηρυκισμόν); 'ἀνάνοντος' is not a Greek word and is likely a print or OCR slip. The citation for this last clause is placed at its end in §19.

title: Works without doctrine, doctrine without works
english: Cyril: …the cud (Leviticus 11:3; Deuteronomy 14:6). For the law calls such animals clean, at least in the sense we have just explained.
Palladius: I understand what you mean.

Cyril: So the law has shown in a riddle the person who is excellent and fully formed in virtue, as in an animal that by nature parts the hoof and brings up the cud. And it teaches in turn that it is good and profitable to make a habit of shaking off the person who is not of this mind, who limps, as it were, toward the good and falls behind in the perfection of virtue. It does this by giving its favorable verdict neither to the animals that bring up the cud without having the parted hoof, nor to those that part the hoof by nature if they do not chew the cud; rather, it records their uncleanness and numbers them among the things that defile (Leviticus 11:4–8). So we affirm, and rightly, that the parting of the foot is a type of practical action and of the quality of our conduct, and in this way we recast into the truth what was said in riddles. And we define the chewing of the cud as a sign of the word that accords with godliness, and of doctrinal knowledge that is both correct and well practiced. Or is it not so?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: Then the one who prides himself on good works but falls short of right doctrine, and does not hold the words of truth in his mind, would rightly be thought incomplete in virtue, and he stands far from deserving admiration. And it is plain that the reverse is also true. For right doctrine and a sweet concern for the divine words would profit us nothing toward being held perfect in virtue if brightness in deeds were not yoked with them. The one who is skilled in both will carry off the verdict of full approval; but for the one who lacks either, whatever admiration he wins for goodness will have no strength. The Savior also points to something of this kind when he says that the one who teaches but does not also do is called least in the kingdom of heaven, while the one who has done and taught is great and distinguished (Matthew 5:19). Under the law, then, the one who falls short in either of the two is unclean. And that we ought to keep away from such people and in no way be seen to have any share with them, the law made clear by saying: ‘You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses’ (Leviticus 11:8). That is, it means that you shall not keep company with them while they live. And if one of them should happen to die, you will keep your own mind undefiled, not so much as touching, so to speak, the things they have produced, that is, their discourses and their foul writings; for such things are the remains of a person’s life.
