Yet handling such remains is just what the untaught heretics are in the habit of doing. For those who became the leaders of the ignorance that is in them have, beyond dispute, gone astray, and they have left with their own disciples what amount to the remains of their own impiety. These disciples welcome them with great delight and take them to live in their minds, and so they carry a stain that is hard to wash off, as though they were handling the flesh of carcasses, which is full of the worst stench and uncleanness.
translator_notes: Opens mid-word, completing ἀνάνον|τος from §18 (read ἀνάγοντος, see §18 note); the citation (Leviticus 11:3; Deuteronomy 14:6) closes the clause begun there. Palladius's 'Πάνυ μὲν οὖν;' carries a question mark in the print, almost certainly a misprint for a full stop; rendered as assent. Matthew 5:19 is cited as Cyril gives it, a paraphrase that differs from the Gospel: Matthew calls least the one who breaks a commandment and teaches others to do so, and great the one who does and teaches; Cyril applies it to the one who teaches without doing. 'You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses' matches LXX Leviticus 11:8 (compare Deuteronomy 14:8). 'You shall not keep company with them while they live' is Cyril's gloss (φησί, 'it means'), not a quotation, so it carries no citation. λογίων is rendered 'discourses' (their written or spoken sayings), not 'oracles'. 'The word that accords with godliness' (λόγος κατ' εὐσέβειαν) may echo 1 Timothy 6:3 (τῇ κατ' εὐσέβειαν διδασκαλίᾳ); uncited.

title: Camel, hare, rock badger and pig
english: Palladius: True.

Cyril: As an example of the animal that does not part the hoof yet brings up the cud, then, the law takes the camel, a strong and very large beast, and the hare and the rock badger, which look smaller, one might say, than all the others (Leviticus 11:4–6). In this way, I think, it took in everything at once by means of the extremes, and left out nothing that lies between them. It is as though one were to say: ‘From the very high and the highest of all, down to the small and the very lowest, everyone who is like this is loathsome and unclean.’ For there is no partiality with God, as it is written (Romans 2:11). If someone is great and proud, raised high by wealth and worldly glory, he will receive a verdict without honor or reward if he is liable to the charges of wickedness. And if someone is small, living with poverty and obscurity, he will be condemned as unclean unless he can boast of a virtuous way of life. Nor could anyone turn his lowliness into a pretext for claiming that the just Judge must have mercy on him, if he lacks what is fitting in deeds, that is, in deeds of godliness and virtue. So the camel, the hare and the rock badger would be a clear type of small and great alike. The law also brings forward the pig as unclean, because it parts the hoof but is not made by nature to chew its food again, that is, to bring up the cud (Leviticus 11:7). In this way it shows that boasting in works is feeble and useless without the word that accords with godliness. For just as faith without works is dead (James 2:26), so the reverse is also true: good order of life and decency in deeds are surely dead when the knowledge of God is absent and the word of godliness has not made its home in our souls. This good order stays low; it is bent toward the earth, and seems somehow afraid to lift its eye upward. We shall find not a few who have suffered something of this kind. At times they lead a dignified and pure life, but because they have not come to know the One who is God by nature and in truth, they fix the eye of their mind, as it were, on earthly things alone. Such a person, too, is unclean; for ‘no one is crowned unless he competes according to the rules,’ as it is written (2 Timothy 2:5).
Palladius: So the law counts us defiled, under the figure of the pig and of the other animals as well, once we have come under its charges.

Cyril: You have put it quite rightly. And the law is not content to set before us images of the unclean through these animals alone. It has chosen rather to benefit us through the whole of creation, as it were, and sets out in rich measure the knowledge of what is useful and fitting. So it goes through the kinds of water creatures too, and the flocks of birds, so that by carefully examining what is natural to each, we may be able to discern what, then, is pleasing to God and what is rejected and hateful to him, and so, by practicing a life fully in keeping with the law, may flee with all our strength from everything that usually defiles. Now the law has spoken…
translator_notes: Leviticus 11:4–6 names the camel, the hare (δασύπους) and the χοιρογρύλλιος; the last is rendered 'rock badger' (the hyrax, as in many English Bibles; older versions say 'coney'); Cyril then calls the hare λαγώς. Leviticus 11:7 is the pig. Deuteronomy 14:7–8 gives the same list; Book 14 follows Leviticus, so Leviticus is cited. 'No partiality with God' matches Romans 2:11 word for word (compare Deuteronomy 10:17, Acts 10:34). 'Faith without works is dead' is closest to James 2:26 (also 2:17, 2:20). 'The just Judge' may echo 2 Timothy 4:8; uncited. 'Such goodness stays below… afraid to lift its eye upward': the feminine participle (οὖσα) refers to εὐκοσμία, the 'good order of life', but the picture is the pig's, which looks only at the ground; kept as Cyril has it. In Palladius's reply the subject of καταμιαίνει is taken to be the law ('counts us defiled'). In Cyril's reply the print reads διὰ δέ γε δὴ μόνων καὶ τῶν τοιῶνδε τυχόν, which does not construe as it stands; the sense 'not through these alone, but through the whole of creation' is plain from the following clause and is followed here. The section ends mid-sentence ('Ἔφη τοίνυν ὁ νόμος', completed in §21).

title: Fish with fins and scales, and creatures of the mud
english: Cyril: …again, in words like these: ‘And these you shall eat of all that are in the waters: all that have fins and scales in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, these you shall eat. But all that have neither fins nor scales in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, of all that the waters bring forth and of every living creature in the water, it is an abomination, and they shall be abominations to you. You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall abhor their carcasses. All that have neither fins nor scales, of the things in the waters, this is an abomination to you’ (Leviticus 11:9–12).
Palladius: But you yourself should explain what the difference is among these, I mean as spiritual contemplation reads them; for I hardly understand it at all.

Cyril: Certainly. I shall tell you as best I can, recasting into plain terms what the law has taken up by way of examples. Those creatures in the waters that the Creator of all has fashioned well after the pattern of fishes are always rowing their way along, as it were, by thrusting out their fins, and they move strongly and very swiftly wherever they may choose. When the sun sends the warm stroke of its rays down into the waters from above, they swim upward and all but dare to leap out of the water itself, refusing to stay below always; and they easily slip through the nets of those who hunt them. But those that are not furnished with scales and fins (those, that is, that live in hard casings and are clothed in a shell that grows with them) know almost nothing of what is above. They are always creeping down into the weeds at the bottom, and they love to linger in muddy places. They are sluggish and easily caught, and anyone who has once caught sight of them can take them without the least effort. That is the plain and true account of those creatures. Now let us go on, as from images and types, to what is clearer.
Palladius: You would do well to explain it, and to go on with it gladly.

Cyril: The Psalmist, pointing out to us with fine wit the distractions of this life and the bitter flood and confusion of affairs within it, sings: ‘This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number, living creatures small and great’ (Psalm 104:25). For we must surely liken to fishes those who at times dart this way and that for nothing needed for their good, and gather only such things as prove them fleshly and set them to endure pointless toil.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: The disciple of Christ also rebukes such people somewhere, speaking in this way: ‘Come now, you who say, “Today and tomorrow we will go into such and such a city and spend a year there, and trade and make a profit”’ (James 4:13). And a little later (James 4:15–16): ‘Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, and…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §20 ends 'Now the law has spoken' (Ἔφη τοίνυν ὁ νόμος) and §21 completes it with ὡδί πη πάλιν ('again, in words like these'). The Leviticus 11:9–12 quotation follows the LXX closely (χείμαρροι, 'streams' or 'torrents'; 'of all that the waters bring forth', ἐρεύγεται, literally 'belch forth'). 'This is the sea, great and wide…' is LXX Psalm 103:25, English Psalm 104:25; ὁ Μελῳδός ('the Singer') is David, rendered 'the Psalmist'. 'Come now, you who say…' is James 4:13 (ὁ τοῦ Χριστοῦ μαθητής, 'the disciple of Christ', is James). The section breaks inside James 4:15 ('If the Lord wills, and…'); the quotation runs on through James 4:16 in §22, so the citation is placed at its start here and should be repeated or closed in §22. In 'gather only such things as prove them fleshly and set them to endure pointless toil' the Greek (ὅσαπερ ἂν ἀποφῆναι σαρκικοὺς καὶ εἰκαίους ἀνατλῆναι παρασκευάζει πόνους) is awkward, with ἀποφῆναι left without a clear governing verb; the sense is taken as 'show them to be fleshly and prepare them to bear pointless labors'. Shellfish and other unscaled sea creatures are described as wearing a shell 'that grows with them' (συμφυές).

title: Scales and fins: those who hide their faults and lift their minds; the shameless are unclean
english: Cyril: …we will live, and we will do this or that.” But as it is, you boast in your arrogance’ (James 4:15–16). So then, like fish, we swim through this broad and spacious sea, that is, the world (Psalm 104:25); for each person’s life differs in some way. For some have not wholly given themselves over to sin. They know, indeed, that at times they are weak and held by the greedy cravings of the flesh, and they do not claim to be clear of other faults either; for ‘we all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2), as it is written. All the same, they shake off as something ugly any wish to behave shamefully with nothing to cover them, and no one could persuade them to practice their wrongdoing openly and without concealment. They take great care to escape notice; for ‘the wise will hide their own shame’ (Proverbs 12:16), as it is written. This, I think, is what it means to have scales as a kind of covering. They also very often swim up toward the heights; for they do not always look downward, but also set their minds on the things above (Colossians 3:2), and they easily slip away from those who would wish to net them for destruction. This, one may say, is to use fins, as it were, in a spiritual sense, and to make the movement of the mind very fervent.
Palladius: What you say is reasonable; for the riddle does in some way lead one to think that the meaning runs this way.

Cyril: But some sin with no restraint, practicing their wickedness naked, as it were, and wholly uncovered; and of them it may well be said, ‘Their glory is in their shame’ (Philippians 3:19). For they are always bent toward uncleanness, and as they wallow in the lowest mire they are in truth brute beasts, or something other than that. Such people would be utterly feeble in every way and easily caught, ruled like slaves of a tyrant by pleasures that lead to every kind of outrage. Or is not the life of those given up as lost something like this? Lewd women and harlots, the utterly shameful and most counterfeit tribe of effeminate men, those who make a name for themselves on the stage, those whose love of the flesh cannot be satisfied, and those who love to wander off into profane idolatry: all these live a truly accursed life, a life that sinks into the most shameful defilements. So the law declares clean those who have been weak in human ways but have not yet turned aside altogether; who swim up, as it were, toward the heights, and have not settled on earthly things alone, but have also set their minds on the things above, and are divided, as it were, between God and the world. But it declares unclean those who give themselves over entirely to choosing, without ceasing, both to do and to think the things of the flesh and of the world; who in these matters have stripped off all shame and are used to behaving shamefully, naked and undisguised. And it usefully removes us from fellowship with these, while not dishonoring fellowship with the former. For to walk the same road as the wicked is not safe; but with those…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation (James 4:13–16 begins in section 21) and mid-turn of Cyril; it carries the ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label used by the other rows of this book, and the inner and outer quotation marks close those opened in section 21. The sea image echoes Psalm 104:25 (LXX 103:25), quoted in section 21. The old English swapped the two references: ‘we all stumble in many ways’ is James 3:2; ‘the wise will hide their own shame’ is a loose quotation closest in sense to Proverbs 12:16 (LXX: the prudent man hides his own dishonour), though its opening words match LXX Proverbs 10:14 (‘the wise will hide perception’). ‘They do not claim to be clear of other faults’ takes βούλονται + ἀφεστάναι as ‘mean/claim’; a more literal sense is ‘they do not wish to stand apart from the other charges’. ‘Set their minds on the things above’ (τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖν) is cited at its first occurrence (Colossians 3:2); the repeat later in the section is left uncited. ‘The things of the flesh’ (τὰ σαρκός φρονεῖν) may echo Romans 8:5 but is left uncited as doubtful. κνώδαλα is rendered ‘brute beasts’; ‘or something other than that’ renders ἤγουν ἕτερόν τι παρὰ τοῦτο, whose referent is unclear (perhaps ‘other than fish’ in the type). ‘Removes us’: the Greek has no expressed object. καθαρίζει / καταμιαίνει are rendered ‘declares clean / declares unclean’, since the law’s verdict on clean and unclean creatures is meant. The section ends mid-sentence; it completes in section 23.

title: Keep good company; the unclean birds, and the proud who soar on high
english: Cyril: …who are more upright it is safe. For it is written: ‘He who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be known’ (Proverbs 13:20). And Paul too writes: ‘If anyone called a brother is greedy, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a swindler, do not even eat with such a one’ (1 Corinthians 5:11).
Palladius: Well said; for the matter is not without profit.

Cyril: This, then, is what the law tells us in riddles about creatures that swim and live in the waters. Then, widening, as it were, the range of examples it sets before us, it goes on to the flocks of birds, saying: ‘And these you shall abhor among the birds, and they shall not be eaten; they are an abomination: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the sea eagle, the vulture, the kite and its kind, the ostrich, the owl, the gull and its kind, every raven and its kind, the hawk and its kind, the night raven, the cormorant, the ibis, the purple gallinule, the pelican, the swan, the heron, the plover and its kind, the hoopoe and the bat (Leviticus 11:13–19). And all winged creeping things that go on all fours are an abomination to you (Leviticus 11:20). But these you shall eat among the winged creeping things that go on all fours: those that have legs above their feet, with which to leap on the ground. These you shall eat of them: the young locust and its kind, the cricket and its kind, the grasshopper and its kind, and the locust and its kind (Leviticus 11:21–22). Every winged creeping thing that has four feet is an abomination to you, and by these you shall be defiled. Whoever touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 11:23–24). Is the meaning of these words clear to you?
Palladius: Not in the least.
Cyril: Do you not perceive by now that, just as with the others, the traits that belong by nature to each of the creatures named would be images of characters and of different ways of life?
Palladius: What do you mean?
Cyril: Shall we take them one at a time, distinguishing each with care?
Palladius: By all means.

Cyril: The law, then, rejects the eagle, the bearded vulture, the sea eagle, and the vulture as well. For birds like these fly about on high; they love to pride themselves on the loftiest heights, and they hate what is low. ‘The young of the vulture,’ it says, ‘fly to the heights’ (Job 5:7). Such, in a way, is the boaster, the man of overweening haughtiness, who has his mind lifted up within himself, who is used to looking down on a gentle and moderate frame of mind, and who has no love at all for associating with the lowly (Romans 12:16). Together with these the law also condemns the kite and its kind, and the raven and its kind. By these it signifies very well the kind of people who know how to plunder and are clever at wrongdoing: the kite is a type of the first, and the deep, jet-black raven of the second. For those who are shrewd…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence (‘but with those who are more upright it is safe’ begins in section 22), so the first paragraph carries the ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label. Proverbs 13:20 follows the LXX (‘will be known’); the Hebrew has ‘will suffer harm’. Cyril’s 1 Corinthians 5:11 omits ‘sexually immoral’ from Paul’s list; the omission is kept. Leviticus 11:13–24 is quoted from the LXX, with Cyril’s own order of birds (ostrich, owl and gull come before the raven) and insects (ophiomaches before akris); citations are placed by verse groups. Bird and insect names follow the LXX terms, whose identities are uncertain: γρύψ (literally ‘griffin’, Hebrew peres) is rendered ‘bearded vulture’ to keep it distinct from γύψ ‘vulture’; στρουθός in Leviticus 11:16 renders the Hebrew for ostrich and is so translated, though the word can mean ‘sparrow’; καταράκτης ‘cormorant’; χαραδριός ‘plover’ (possibly the nocturnal stone curlew, which fits Cyril’s night birds in section 24); βροῦχος, ἀττάκης, ὀφιομάχης (‘snake fighter’) and ἀκρίς are given as young locust, cricket, grasshopper and locust only as distinct English labels. Job 5:7 is the LXX (‘the young of the vulture fly to the heights’); the Hebrew reads ‘as the sparks fly upward’. ‘Associating with the lowly’ alludes to Romans 12:16 (τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγόμενοι). ‘The raven’ is supplied for ὁ μελάντατος καὶ βαθύς (‘the blackest and deep one’), which refers back to the raven just named; ‘deep’ keeps the hint of hidden cunning taken up in section 24. οἱ δριμεῖς is ‘the shrewd’. The section ends mid-word (δρι|μεῖς); the sentence completes in section 24.

title: Greedy, cruel and night-loving birds; great and small alike condemned
english: Cyril: …in wickedness are in some way dark and not plain to all, and they keep the baseness of their character hidden within themselves, out of sight of the many. In those who are sick with the accursed disease of arrogance there always grows up beside it the wish to take advantage of whomever they can, to besiege them with wicked devices of every kind, and so to plunder them, and that insatiably. That is why it adds at once: ‘And the ostrich and the gull’ (Leviticus 11:16). For these, I think, are most insatiable, always gathering up whatever comes their way. Then it says: ‘And the hawk and its kind, the night raven, the cormorant, the ibis, the purple gallinule, the pelican and the swan’ (Leviticus 11:16–18). These too would portray in themselves those who plot cruelly and savagely against others and fasten without restraint on whomever they can, so that they do not shrink even from putting some in danger and fear for their very lives. For the hawk swoops fiercely on every weaker bird; it darts at sparrows, and when it catches them it kills them. The cormorant, the ibis and the purple gallinule, and I would add the pelican too, fall furiously on the fish and make their destruction their food. Such, as far as conduct and savagery of character go, are all who count it as nothing to destroy others for the sake of their own pleasure. They have thrust aside the law of mutual love and offended against the ordinances of love, and it would be altogether fitting for them to hear this, even from us: ‘Do not seek your own interests, but also those of others (Philippians 2:4; 1 Corinthians 10:24); for love,’ it says, ‘does no wrong to a neighbor’ (Romans 13:10). Again, it said that one must refuse the owl, the heron, the plover and their kind, the hoopoe and the bat (Leviticus 11:16–19). These, I think, are lovers of the night. They delight in the darkness and are practiced at taking their flight in it as their sweetest pleasure, but they hate the light of the sun and cannot bear to do anything in it. Such birds would plainly stand for those who work evil. For what Christ said is true: ‘Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, that they have been done in God’ (John 3:20–21). The winged creeping things too are unclean, those ‘which go,’ it says, ‘on all fours’ (Leviticus 11:20): for example, the various kinds of flies and anything akin to them. These are countless, small and loathsome, and they cannot fly high. We must therefore look closely at the reason why the law came down even to these. For just as, when it made mention of the beasts, it named the camel and then added the hare (Leviticus 11:4–6), declaring all those charged with wickedness equally unclean, whether one were great or small — for, as it is written, there is no partiality with God (Romans 2:11) — so here too it calls to mind the eagle, naming the most kingly of birds, but then comes down again to the very smallest of winged creatures, putting small and great on an equal footing if one is a worker of outrageous deeds, and so cannot escape the condemnation that is his due. Yet it does set apart from this kind…
translator_notes: Whole section is one continuing turn of Cyril that begins mid-word (δρι|μεῖς), so it carries the ‘Cyril: …’ continuation label. The old English placed John 3:20 beside ‘ostrich and gull’ and 1 Corinthians 10:24 beside the hawk list; both are corrected (Leviticus 11:16; 11:16–18). ‘Do not seek your own interests, but also those of others’ blends 1 Corinthians 10:24 (μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ζητείτω) with the wording of Philippians 2:4 (ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἑτέρων); both are cited. ‘Love does no wrong to a neighbour’ is Romans 13:10. The camel and hare refer back to Cyril’s earlier treatment of the four-footed beasts (Leviticus 11:4–6; λαγωός is Cyril’s word for the animal of 11:6, which the LXX calls δασύπους). ‘No partiality with God’ is Romans 2:11 (compare Acts 10:34). Source has καταθρῶσκε· (OCR punctuation slip) read as καταθρῴσκει; καταῤῥάκτης here and καταράκτης in section 23 are the same bird. στρουθός (Leviticus 11:16) is kept as ‘ostrich’ for consistency with section 23, though Cyril may have understood a small greedy bird; στρουθία, the hawk’s prey, are ‘sparrows’. τὰ μυιῶν is taken as flies (μυῖα). The section ends mid-word (γέ|νους); the object (locust and young locust) follows in section 25. κτηνῶν is ‘the beasts’ (no ‘four-footed’ in the Greek); the Greek parenthesis on Romans 2:11 is set off with dashes to avoid nested brackets.

title: Leaping insects, the worldly man, and washing toward evening
english: Cyril: …the locust and the young locust and creatures like them (Leviticus 11:21–22), because of their strength: they can leap up, they are least inclined to linger below, and they often rise on high and spring easily from place to place. Such, in a way, is the person who lives a worldly life and yet is not wholly without a share of decency in other respects and of love for God. Such a person is not bound altogether to earthly things, nor does he settle among what is below. He has learned in some measure to set his mind on the things above (Colossians 3:2), and at times he wins approval, springing up toward the things above and flying over the things of earth.

As for one who touches unclean things and has been defiled, he must wash his garment, and toward evening, the law says, he will be clean (Leviticus 11:24–25). In this it very aptly points to the mystery of Christ, through whom we have been cleansed and are rich in the forgiveness that comes through holy baptism. This came about, clearly, at the time of his coming, a time that fell, as it were, toward evening, that is, when the present age was already drawing toward its end. Or do we not say that the Word of God became man in the last times?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: The law also says that a person becomes unclean in another way, if he happens to touch a wild beast, or any other of the unclean animals. It speaks thus: ‘Every creature that walks on its paws, among all the beasts that go on all fours, is unclean to you. Everyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening, and whoever carries their carcasses shall wash his garments and be unclean until evening. These are unclean to you (Leviticus 11:27–28). And these are unclean to you among the creeping things on the earth: the weasel, the mouse, the land crocodile, the shrew, the chameleon, the gecko, the lizard, and the mole. These are unclean to you among all the creeping things on the earth. Everyone who touches them when they are dead will be unclean until evening (Leviticus 11:29–31). And anything on which one of them falls when they are dead will be unclean, whether any vessel of wood, or a garment, or a skin, or sackcloth. Every vessel with which any work is done shall be dipped in water, and it will be unclean until evening, and then it will be clean’ (Leviticus 11:32). To these it added that every vessel on which any of their carcasses falls will be defiled, an earthen jar and a leather one, a garment, food and drink, except, it says, a spring of water, a cistern, a gathering of water, and seeds (Leviticus 11:33–37).

Through the wild beasts the law seems to point to the most savage of robbers, who count as nothing even murder, the evil beyond all others, and who all but devour whomever they come upon, destroying without pity, with all mercy cast out. Through the mouse and the weasel, and the creatures close to them and like them (I mean the land crocodile, the lizard and the gecko), it points to the easily startled and cowardly kinds of thieves who prowl about at night. They love to prey unseen on those who are dozing, but they are terribly afraid of being caught, and…
translator_notes: The row opens mid-sentence; sec. 24 ends ‘Ὑπεξάγει γε μὴν τοῦ τοιούτου γέ-’, so the subject of the opening fragment is ‘he exempts from this class’ (the clean leaping insects of Leviticus 11:21–22); the fragment is kept as it falls, with ‘Cyril: …’ as in the sibling chunks. βροῦχος rendered ‘young locust’ (a wingless locust stage; KJV/LXX translators vary: ‘caterpillar’, ‘bald locust’). ‘Toward evening he will be clean’ summarises the repeated ‘unclean until evening’ of Leviticus 11:24–25 (and 11:28, 11:40); cited at its first occurrence. ‘The last times’ (ἐν ἐσχάτοις καιροῖς) echoes Hebrews 1:2 and 1 Peter 1:20 but matches neither exactly, so it is left uncited. ‘Set his mind on the things above’ (τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖν) is a clear echo of Colossians 3:2 and is cited. βέβηλον (‘profane’) is rendered ‘unclean’ since Cyril uses it here as a synonym for ἀκάθαρτος. In the Leviticus list, LXX καλαβώτης and Cyril’s own ἀσκαλαβώτης are both rendered ‘gecko’; ‘walks on its paws’ renders LXX ἐπὶ χειρῶν (‘on hands’). Cyril’s summary after the quotation (earthen jar, leather, garment, food and drink; spring, cistern, gathering of water, seeds exempt) condenses Leviticus 11:33–37 and repeats items of 11:32; the oven of 11:35 is omitted by Cyril. Section ends mid-sentence (‘καὶ’), continued in sec. 26. Pronouns for God are capitalised (‘His coming’) where the referent is Christ; the unnamed subject of φησί/προσετίθει is rendered ‘it’ (the law), matching the end of sec. 24 and secs. 26–27. ψοφοδεῆ rendered ‘easily startled’ (literally ‘afraid of noise’), which sec. 26 picks up with ‘if anyone makes a noise’.

title: Robbers, thieves, and the company that defiles
english: Cyril: …they shun the watchfulness of those they wrong. Are not the weasel and the mouse most thievish creatures, and quick to take fright? Do they not dive into their holes in the ground if anyone makes a noise? And would not they, and the land crocodile and its kin, far rather feed by night than by day?
Palladius: True.

Cyril: So everything of the robber’s kind is unclean, whether a man has a beast’s ways and bloodthirsty hands, or whether he pilfers small things, like the mouse and the weasel, and, after the manner of the mole and the gecko, springs up walls and onto roofs. And if anyone touches those so defiled, he will share in their guilt, for fellowship with such people makes those who share it wholly and altogether unclean. The defiled vessels would stand as a type of human beings, for man has the form of a vessel. Yet the law frees a spring of water, a cistern and a gathering of water from having to be defiled, even if something defiled under the law should happen to fall into them. In this, I think, it does not let those under the law consider the matter altogether burdensome and hard to carry through, or find the keeping of the law impossible to practice, as they would if they suffered harm here, in their most vital needs. For at times they would have had to leave their cities and houses, since their water would have been defiled and they would have lost a use they needed and could not do without. So the law relaxed the strictness of its literal rule for the sake of what was necessary and useful for those under the law.
Palladius: The argument is persuasive.

Cyril: Yet it says that even the carcass of a clean animal is unclean, just as the others are, and it added that this too will defile whoever touches it. It writes thus: ‘If one of the cattle that you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass will be unclean until evening; and whoever eats of its carcass shall wash his garments, and be unclean until evening, and bathe in water, and be clean. And whoever carries its carcass shall wash his garments, and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 11:39–40). This, I think, is plainly the same as the saying: ‘If anyone who bears the name of brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or a reviler, or a robber, do not even eat with such a one’ (1 Corinthians 5:11). For if anyone at all who is held in esteem for holiness, who has already been cleansed and received through faith into spiritual fellowship, undergoes the deadness that comes from sin, ‘let him be loathsome,’ it says, ‘and hated.’ For, defiled by dead works, he surely defiles whoever clings to him. But if anyone does suffer that defilement, let him become clean through water toward evening; and what this means, our argument has already shown us plainly. Notice too that the law says the one who eats…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing the thieves who ‘dread being caught, and shun…’ from sec. 25. Cyril’s claim that the mole and gecko climb walls and roofs is kept as he gives it (the gecko does; the mole is his own addition). ‘Makes those who share it wholly and altogether unclean’: ἀποφαίνει has no stated object beside the plural ἀκαθάρτους; ‘those who share it’ supplies the sense. ‘Man has the form of a vessel’ may echo 2 Timothy 2:20–21 or 2 Corinthians 4:7, but no text is quoted, so it is left uncited. ἱστορία here means the literal, historical level of the law, rendered ‘its literal rule’. ‘Let him be loathsome and hated’ (βδελυρὸς ἔστω… καὶ ἀπηχθημένος) is introduced with φησί but matches no verse I can identify; it may be Cyril’s paraphrase of the Levitical ‘abomination’ language (Leviticus 11:10–13, 11:41–43), so it is left uncited. ‘Dead works’ echoes Hebrews 6:1 and 9:14 but is a stock phrase here, so uncited. ‘Clings to him’ (κολλώμενον) may glance at 1 Corinthians 6:16–17; uncited. ‘What this means, our argument has already shown’ refers back to the evening washing as baptism in sec. 25. The section ends mid-word (θνησι-|μαίων); the English breaks after ‘the one who eats…’ and sec. 27 resumes with ‘of their carcasses’. The land crocodile clause (κροκόδειλός τε χερσαῖος καὶ τὰ συγγενῆ) is a further subject of νέμοιντο, not a comparison, and the sentence stays a question as in the Greek.

title: Keep clear of the dead; the burning bush and the sandal
english: Cyril: …of their carcasses will be unclean, and so will anyone who only touches them. It does not free from blame and accusation the one who has shared in their deadness, nor does it call anyone guiltless even if he only comes close and draws near. For I think we must soberly keep away not only from doing the same deeds as the wicked, but even from merely keeping company with them. ‘For whoever touches pitch will be defiled,’ it says (Sirach 13:1). And the saying is true. That the law took up the lessons of these examples for the forming of character, one may learn from what follows. For it said again: ‘You shall not make your souls loathsome with any of the creeping things that creep on the earth, and you shall not be defiled by them, and you shall not be unclean through them; for I am the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 11:43–44). For what defilement could an animal’s dying, or touching what has died, bring upon the human soul? What harm could food do, which goes into the belly and is sent out into the drain, as the Savior said (Matthew 15:17)?
Palladius: None, I think; you understand it rightly.

Cyril: Then I say that we must, like the most skillful sailors, crowd on every sail and run clear of defilements, and put in to the life most dear to God as to a calm shore where no waves break. For God could become approachable to us in this way alone and in no other, and that this is true is easy to see. For it is written again in Exodus: ‘Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the sheep into the wilderness and came to Mount Horeb. And an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the bush, and he saw that the bush was burning with fire, yet the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, “I will turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush is not consumed.” When the Lord saw that he was drawing near to look, the Lord called to him out of the bush, saying, “Moses, Moses.” And he said, “What is it?” And he said, “Do not come near here; take the sandal off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground”’ (Exodus 3:1–5). Do you see, then, that no one could come near the all-pure God without first washing every stain from his own soul, and freeing his foot from all the deadness that lies in deeds? By the foot I mean the spiritual walk by which we go toward what must be done. For is not the sandal the remains of a dead animal?
Palladius: Of course it is.

Cyril: Then the sandal is a type of deadness. If anyone throws off this deadness like a load and breaks the bonds that would be his ruin, he will come near and belong to God, and from then on he will be fit to save others as well. So it was that Moses was appointed to be sent out, and to redeem the sons of Israel. And a sacred saying has told us: ‘Son, if you become wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbor’ (Proverbs 9:12).
Palladius: Well said.
translator_notes: Opens mid-word (‘…μαίων αὐτῶν’), completing ‘the one who eats of their carcasses’ from sec. 26 (Leviticus 11:40, already cited there). ‘For whoever touches pitch will be defiled’ is Sirach 13:1 (LXX ὁ ἁπτόμενος πίσσης μολυνθήσεται), cited by its English name Sirach. ‘You shall not make your souls loathsome’ follows LXX Leviticus 11:43 (Cyril reads βδελύξεσθε for the LXX’s βδελύξητε; same sense). The Saviour’s saying about food going into the belly and out into the drain is Matthew 15:17 (εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται); Mark 7:19 is parallel but uses different wording, so only Matthew is cited. ‘Crowd on every sail’ renders the proverb πάντα κάλων σείειν (‘shake out every rope’, to use every effort); the participle σείοντας belongs to ‘we’, not to the sailors, so the English makes us the ones who set sail. Προσιτὸς has no expressed subject; God is supplied from the sense and the following Exodus proof. LXX ὑπὸ τὴν ἔρημον rendered ‘into the wilderness’; ‘Παρελθὼν ὄψομαι’ rendered ‘I will turn aside and see’ (literally ‘passing by’). Proverbs 9:12 is quoted in its LXX form (‘Son… and for your neighbour’), which differs from the Hebrew-based English but has the same verse number. ‘So it was that Moses was appointed’ renders γοῦν with imperfect προσεχειρίζετο; ‘to redeem’ renders εἰς… ἐκλύτρωσιν. νοητήν (of the ‘walk’) rendered ‘spiritual’, Cyril’s usual contrast with the bodily foot. ἥν (‘which if one unloads’) refers to νεκρότητος, so ‘throws off this deadness like a load’ names the referent.

title: Made ready to see God: Sinai and the circumcision of Abraham
english: Cyril: Well then, shall we not add this point to these as well?
Palladius: Which one?

Cyril: When God, who rules over all, was about to come down on Mount Sinai in the form of fire (Exodus 19:18), Moses was commanded to make Israel ready to see God. The manner of the preparation the Master of all laid down himself. For the Lord said to Moses: ‘Go down and solemnly charge the people, and purify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments, and let them be ready for the third day; for on the third day the Lord will come down on Mount Sinai before all the people’ (Exodus 19:10–11). Those, then, who long for close fellowship with God, and whose aim is, as it were, to stand before him and serve him with strength and eagerness for every good thing, must first be purified. Such a person would then be quite fit even for this: that he too should already, in some way, behold God, according to the Savior’s word: ‘For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew 5:8).

Again, if you wish, you will see the divine Abraham himself advanced to this same splendor. Come, let us recount in turn what concerns him. For it is written thus: ‘And the Lord said to Abraham: As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you, throughout their generations. And this is the covenant that you shall keep between me and you, and between your offspring after you, throughout their generations: every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. A child of eight days shall be circumcised among you, every male, throughout your generations, both the one born in your house and the one bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring. The one born in your house and the one bought with money shall surely be circumcised. And my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from its kindred, because he has broken my covenant’ (Genesis 17:9–14). Then it says: ‘And Abraham took Ishmael his son, and all those born in his house, and all those bought with his money, and every male among the men of his house, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskin on that very day, as God had spoken to him’ (Genesis 17:23).

What, then, was the reward of his obedience, and in what way did circumcision benefit him? We shall learn from what follows. ‘For God appeared to him,’ it says, ‘by the oak of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent at midday. And he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing near him. And when he saw them, he ran from the door of his tent to meet them, and bowed down to the ground (Genesis 18:1–2), and said…
translator_notes: Exodus 19:18 cited as a clear allusion for God descending 'in the form of fire' on Sinai. The quotation at Genesis 17:9 reads Κύριος where the LXX has ὁ Θεός; translated as printed ('the Lord'). Genesis 17 quotation follows the LXX closely (ἐκ τοῦ γένους αὐτῆς rendered 'from its kindred'; διεσκέδασεν 'has broken'). εἰστήκεισαν ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ rendered 'standing over against him' (LXX idiom for standing near, not literally above). The Genesis 18 quotation runs on across the section break: the source splits the word Κύ|ριε, so 'and said:' closes section 28 and the address 'Lord' opens section 29. θεσπέσιος rendered 'divine' to match the rest of the book.

title: True circumcision opens the way to God; the story of Dinah begins
english: Cyril: ‘…Lord, if indeed I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant. Let water be brought, and let them wash your feet, and refresh yourselves under the tree; and I will bring bread, and you shall eat; and after this you shall go on your way, since it is for this that you have turned aside to your servant. And they said: We will do so, as you have said’ (Genesis 18:3–5).

For circumcision in the flesh would be a very clear type of the inward circumcision, the circumcision in the spirit (Romans 2:29), by which Christ removes all defilement from our thoughts. For, in the words of the blessed Paul, ‘we have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the flesh’ (Colossians 2:11). For when we have, as it were, stripped off the old self, which is being corrupted by deceitful desires (Ephesians 4:22), and have all but cut away the pleasures of the flesh by the keen edge and the working of the Spirit, we shall already, in some measure, show ourselves fit to be counted worthy even of seeing God, and of becoming a sacred dwelling place of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. ‘For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this generation, we will come, I and the Father, and make our home with him, and dwell in him,’ said the Savior (Mark 8:38; John 14:23).

Nor does the reward of goodness stop there. Rather, as those already received into close fellowship with God, we shall come to know the things that are in him, through the revelation that comes from him, of course; just as the divine Abraham too was taught about the overthrow of Sodom (Genesis 18:17–21). For God shared his counsel with him as with a friend. See, then, that to be rid of defilements would bring us in return countless good things. Therefore Paul too says: ‘I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, well pleasing to God, which is your reasonable worship’ (Romans 12:1). And indeed the prophet Jeremiah cried out plainly: ‘Wash your heart clean of wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be saved’ (Jeremiah 4:14).
Palladius: We must approach the all-holy God, then, not with a profaned soul, but in a holy and blameless life. For in this way we shall go straight to what is fitting.

Cyril: Quite so, Palladius. And I think it will take you no great labor to see that what is said on this point holds true, if you choose to search into the lives of the saints with a love of learning and with a mind that agrees with mine. For the divine Paul said that the things that befell those of old as types were written down as a way of admonishing us (1 Corinthians 10:11). That we must approach God pure and washed, then, one could learn once more from the following as well. For Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, being a virgin and of an age for marriage, ran out of her father’s tent to look at the daughters of the people of Shechem (Genesis 34:1). But Shechem, the son of Hamor, did not keep still. He at once fell in love with the girl (Genesis 34:3) and was swept away by unrestrained desires toward what he had set his mind on. Going about it rather brutishly, the foreigner, who was still uncircumcised, forced the Hebrew virgin (Genesis 34:2). The sons of Jacob found the matter unbearable (Genesis 34:7), and by the law of war they fell upon those who had impiously outraged a Hebrew woman, their own sister (Genesis 34:25–29). As for the divine Jacob, who was distressed and terrified, and who feared that he would be utterly destroyed…
translator_notes: DOUBTFUL READING (needs editorial decision): the Savior's saying is printed as 'Ὃς γὰρ ἂν ἐπαισχυνθῇ με καὶ τοὺς ἐμοὺς λόγους ἐν τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ, ἐλευσόμεθα ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ, καὶ μονὴν παρ' αὐτῷ ποιησόμεθα, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ καταλύσομεν.' The opening clause is Mark 8:38 ('whoever is ashamed of me and my words in this generation'), which contradicts the promise that follows; the promise is John 14:23 ('if anyone loves me he will keep my word ... we will come to him and make our home with him'), with an added 'and dwell in him'. Both the Migne PDF text and the cleaned text read the same, so this is the printed text, not an OCR slip; Cyril's argument needs John 14:23, and the print may have lost or garbled the conditional. Translated exactly as printed, with both references cited; consider a note or a check of the critical text before publishing. Genesis 18:5 reply: the source reads ποιήσομεν ('we will do'), LXX ποίησον ('do'); translated as printed. Colossians 2:11 is quoted in shortened form (LXX/NT 'the body of the flesh' becomes 'the flesh'). 'τοῦ πνεύματος' in 'keenness and working of the Spirit' could mean the human spirit set against the flesh; capitalized as the Holy Spirit, which suits Cyril's usage, but this is a judgment. 'Inward circumcision ... in the spirit' (νοητῆς καὶ ἐν πνεύματι) is cited to Romans 2:29 by the reviewer as a clear Pauline allusion (circumcision of the heart, in the spirit). 'God shared His counsel with him as with a friend' may echo Abraham as 'friend of God' (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23); left uncited. Sodom revelation cited to Genesis 18:17–21 (God's disclosure to Abraham). λογικὴν λατρείαν rendered 'reasonable worship' to keep λατρεία = worship, the title word of the work. πολυτείας is read as πολιτείας ('lives, conduct'). The Dinah narrative is Cyril's paraphrase of Genesis 34, not a quotation; citations mark the verses paraphrased. ὁμοφρόνως rendered 'with a mind that agrees with mine' (or 'in a like spirit'). The last sentence runs on across the section break (διόλ|λυσθαι); the main clause 'God received him' opens section 30.

title: Jacob purifies his house before Bethel; clothed in a clean life
english: Cyril: …with all his family, God received him and saved him once more; and it is worth seeing how. It is written thus: ‘And Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: You have made me hateful, so that I am odious to all who live in the land, among both the Canaanites and the Perizzites; and I am few in number; they will gather against me and cut me down, and I shall be wiped out, I and my house. But they said: No, they have treated our sister like a prostitute’ (Genesis 34:30–31). ‘And God said to Jacob: Arise, go up to the place Bethel, and dwell there; and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from the face of Esau your brother. And Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him: Put away from among you the gods that are with you, and purify yourselves, and change your garments; and let us arise and go up to Bethel, and let us make there an altar to the God who heard me in the day of affliction, who was with me and kept me safe on the way by which I went. And they gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands, and the earrings that were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the terebinth that is in Shechem, and destroyed them, to this day’ (Genesis 35:1–4).

You see that the Master of all received the righteous man in his terror, and commanded him to build an altar for a pleasing aroma and as a splendid votive offering for the salvation and help that would be his. And Jacob, knowing well that this had to be done, commands them first to purify themselves, putting away the falsely named gods from among them and changing into other garments. But this, I think, would at once signify sincerity in faith and a life kept free from profanation. For to love to cleave to God single-mindedly, not divided in mind, nor inclined to remain sick with the remnants of the demons’ deceit, may fittingly be understood in the removal of the foreign gods; and in the changing of garments, the putting on, as it were, of a pure way of life.

For this is how the most wise Paul too saw fit to write. Or do you not hear him saying plainly: ‘Put off the old self, which is being corrupted by deceitful desires (Ephesians 4:22), and put on the new self, which is being renewed after the image of its Creator’ (Colossians 3:10)? And by ‘the putting off of the flesh’ he means the laying aside of fleshly pleasures (Colossians 2:11). Solomon too writes somewhere: ‘At all times let your garments be bright’ (Ecclesiastes 9:8). I would say that our wise Solomon, who understood very rightly, would not go so far in trifling as to urge us to revel childishly in bright clothes; rather, he likens to a bright robe the life that is, so to speak, washed clean and free from all filth. Otherwise, how could anyone put on our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:14)? Would you not say, my friend, that one who is clothed in the glories of the gospel way of life surely achieves just that?
Palladius: Very much so.
translator_notes: The quotation runs Genesis 34:30–31 straight into Genesis 35:1–4 without a break in the source; split into two citations. At Genesis 35:2 Cyril's text reads 'the gods that are with you' (without ἀλλοτρίους, which the LXX has); translated as printed; 35:4 has 'foreign gods'. 'And destroyed them to this day' is the LXX addition to Genesis 35:4, kept. 'For a fragrant aroma' (εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας) is stock sacrificial language from the Pentateuch, not a single allusion; uncited. Paul's 'Put off the old self ... put on the new' conflates Ephesians 4:22 (ἀποθέσθαι, 'corrupted according to the desires of deceit') with Colossians 3:10 ('renewed after the image of its Creator'); both cited. ἀπέκθεσιν (both witnesses) is read as ἀπέκδυσιν, the word of Colossians 2:11 already quoted in section 29; the Colossians citation marks that reference. Ecclesiastes 9:8 LXX reads λευκά ('white'); Cyril has λαμπρά ('bright'), translated as printed. ὦ τᾶν rendered 'my friend'. The closing clause 'brings this about in full' renders ἀποπεραίνει ... πάντως τὸ χρῆμα (accomplishes the thing, putting on Christ).

title: Joseph refuses Potiphar's wife
english: Cyril: And if one turns to the celebrated Joseph himself, he will find that Joseph neglected no part of uprightness, but understood that God would work with him in anything at all and come to his help, if he refused outright to let himself be defiled. For he could have prospered and given himself up to luxuries, letting himself run with the fiery leaps of youth toward whatever was sweet and dear, and be carried along by impulses that no one rebuked. This he did not do; far from it. Instead he reckoned the portion that is with God the better, as it were, and preferred the labors of self-control to everything that pampers for the moment. For he knew that the stirring of the flesh is somehow sweet at first and bewitches the mind as if with honey, so far as there is pleasure in such things; yet in the end it turns to what is no longer sweet. For at once penalties and punishments, and every evil of that kind, will hang over the head of the one who has sinned. Shall we recount a few of the things written about him?
Palladius: By all means.

Cyril: ‘And Joseph,’ it says, ‘was handsome in form and very beautiful in appearance. And after these things his master’s wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, “Lie with me.” But he would not, and he said to his master’s wife, “If because of me my master knows nothing of what is in his house, and he has given into my hands all that he has, and nothing in this house is above me, and nothing has been kept back from me except you, because you are his wife, how then shall I do this evil thing and sin before God?” And as she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to sleep with her and be with her. Then a certain day came, and Joseph went into the house to do his work, and none of the household was inside; and she caught hold of him by his garments, saying, “Lie with me.” And leaving his garments in her hands, he fled and went outside. And when she saw that he had left his garments in her hands and fled and gone outside, she called those who were in the house and spoke to them, saying, “See, he has brought in a Hebrew servant to us to make sport of us. He came in to me, saying, ‘Lie with me,’ and I cried out with a loud voice. And when he heard that I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garments with me and fled and went outside.”’ (Genesis 39:6–15) You see how the wretched woman tried to force him to her bed against his will, yet his mind stood firm in self-control and was overcome by nothing at all? He was still a lad, only about seventeen years old (Genesis 37:2), with his first beard just coming, at the height of pleasure, amid the most fiery stirrings and, if we may put it so, amid hard desires that heed no warning. For youth is always somehow given to impulses of craving that are still unbroken, and it does not readily bear the bridles that lead to self-control.
translator_notes: The Greek of this section breaks mid-word at the column change (τὸ ἔφ|ηβον); the whole closing sentence ('For youth is always somehow prone ... bridles that lead to self-control') is rendered here at the end of section 31, so section 32 begins with the next sentence. The quotation is Genesis 39:6b-15 LXX (it begins with the second half of verse 6, 'And Joseph was handsome in form'); English Bible numbering is the same. The LXX 'this evil word' (τὸ ῥῆμα τὸ πονηρόν) is rendered 'this evil thing', the Hebraism's sense. 'Seventeen years' is cited to Genesis 37:2 (Joseph's age when sold); Cyril applies it loosely ('barely about seventeen') to the time of the temptation. ἐπιείκεια rendered 'uprightness' (Cyril's general sense of virtuous conduct), not 'gentleness'. γενικῶς ('generally, in kind') taken as 'outright'. γύναιον is a contemptuous diminutive, rendered 'the wretched woman'. Uncited allusions: the honey that is sweet at first but not in the end recalls Proverbs 5:3-4 (the harlot's lips drip honey, afterward bitter), but the wording is not close enough to cite; 'the portion with God' may echo Luke 10:42 but uses μοῖρα, not μερίς, so no citation.

title: Joseph's reward and David's witness
english: Cyril: But the wondrous Joseph was unshaken. He did not have the loose, undisciplined ways of youth, nor was he afraid because he was a foreigner and a household slave; for he had been forced into both by his brothers when they sold him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:28). And since he was stronger alike than that most loathsome pleasure and than the stirrings toward lewdness, the wretched woman slandered him and turned the charge round against the young man (Genesis 39:17–19). He would not yield to her demands, and she branded him an assailant. From then on the young man was a prisoner (Genesis 39:20); yet by divine grace he was kept safe, and at once he won, as the wage of his self-control, rule over the whole land of the Egyptians (Genesis 41:41). So even if this course brings labors, even if heavy sweat lies before the glories of self-control, it counts for little with one who has chosen to love God wholly. For he will have, yes, he will have praise to match it and rewards of equal weight. That is why the inspired David too marvels at the most praiseworthy young man for what he suffered in this cause, saying, ‘Joseph was sold as a slave; they humbled his feet in fetters; his soul passed through iron’ (Psalm 105:17–18). By iron, I think, he means the hard and unbreakable onset of such sweat, through which one may hold sin in check and depart from all filth, and indeed attain the holy and most pure life, I mean the life of the Gospel, the life in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
translator_notes: Section 32 continues Cyril's speech from section 31 with no new speaker turn; it opens with 'Cyril:' because every section in this book names its speaker; the half-word at the start (ηβον) and its clause are rendered at the end of section 31. Book 14 ends here with the doxology. LXX renumbering: Cyril quotes LXX Psalm 104:17b-18 (Εἰς δοῦλον ἐπράθη Ἰωσήφ ... σίδηρον διῆλθεν ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ), cited as English Psalm 105:17-18; 'his soul passed through iron' follows the LXX (the Hebrew reads differently), and Cyril's comment depends on that wording. The slander ('turned the charge round') is cited to Genesis 39:17-19, where she repeats her accusation to her husband; ὑβριστής (one who commits outrage) rendered 'assailant'. Rule over Egypt cited to Genesis 41:41 ('I have set you over all the land of Egypt'); 41:43 says the same. The historic presents συκοφαντεῖ ... ποιεῖται are rendered in the past tense for English narrative flow. ἱδρῶτες ('sweats') kept as 'sweat' in both places because Cyril's gloss on 'iron' points back to it (τῶν ἱδρώτων); 'sweat before glory' echoes a classical commonplace (Hesiod, Works and Days 289), not Scripture, so no citation. τῶν εἰς ἐγκράτειαν αὐχημάτων ('the boasts toward self-control') rendered 'before one can glory in self-control'. τληπάθεια rendered 'what he suffered'.
